prolog.text:
You live your life at home, suddenly the post comes in you find a letter it says 
something about your grandma Lizzy, YOU NEVER HAD A GRANDMA NAMED LIZZY atleast you didnt know you had one named like that till now.
It says something about a house and that you need to go there in a few days so it wont be demolished from the local town, you see the town, LÜNEN...
That was now 3 weeks ago, you are currently on route to the house, you just drove trough the forest, the navi buzzes "Please turn left... krck" 
the navi abruptly stops. Suddenly you see a few houses first one then two then three and so on, you finally reached the town. 
As you pull up to the driveway you see that the whole house is covered in red and yellow leaves from the nearby trees.
it is night, so you hurry up into the house, noticing that the key is already in the lock, you dont think anything about it and wander inside.

ort.haus.k1.text: The hallway smells sweet, like fruit that has been sitting in a drawer for years, and there's a clean stripe down the middle of the dusty floor, like somebody walks here every day, just not today. Kitchen on the left, stairs on the right, and at the end of the hall a door that stands a finger-width open with warm air coming out of it. The light switch works, which feels like a small miracle. You tell yourself the door is a problem for tomorrow.

optionen.name: Look at the kitchen
optionen.text: One cup stands upside down on a little doily, like it was set out for you, and the kettle next to it is cold but has a fresh drip hanging from the spout. On the shelf there's a biscuit tin with LIZZY scratched into the lid, full of old keys and one photo: a woman with folded hands in front of THIS house, four people next to her, and not one of them smiling.

optionen.name: Touch the cold stretch of wall
optionen.text: One piece of the hallway wall is colder than the rest, like a fridge door. You put your palm flat on it and for a second you swear something on the other side pushes back, soft, about the size of a fist. You pull your hand away and wipe it on your jeans, even though it's dry.

optionen.name: Try the warm door at the end of the hall
optionen.text: The handle is warm like skin. The door opens exactly a finger-width more and then stops, not locked, just STUCK, like it's holding its breath. Somewhere behind it something drips. You take your hand away a bit too fast.

optionen.name: Go upstairs to the bedroom
optionen.text: Every stair screams except the third. The bed is made, the sheets are fresh, and THAT is what bothers you, because nobody has lived here for years. Through the window you see the end of the street and a lake with fog already lying on it.

ort.lunuen.k1.text: Lünen at night is the kind of quiet where you can hear your own jacket. The fog sits at knee height, the curtains are all drawn so tight they look painted on, and on the whole main street you count two people, one with a dog that doesn't bark and one standing at a bus stop where no bus has come in years. Somebody swept the leaves into piles, every pile the same size. The only warm light comes from the little church at the end of the street.

optionen.name: Ask the woman at the bus stop about your grandma
optionen.text: She looks at you a bit too long and says, 'Lizzy was part of it,' like that explains everything. When you ask part of WHAT, she suddenly remembers that her bus is coming. There's no bus. There isn't even a timetable on the pole.

optionen.name: Look at the church window
optionen.text: Behind the yellow glass someone is moving chairs, slowly, one by one, and putting each one back exactly where it was. You can't see a face, only a dark sleeve and calm hands, the hands of someone with all the time in the world.

varianten.wiederbesuch: Lünen again, same fog, same piles of leaves, and you could swear the man with the dog is standing a few steps closer to the church than before. The bus stop is empty now. The church window is dark.

ort.nook.k1.text: The Nook is a tiny wooden hut at the side of the road, built by somebody who clearly had no plan but a LOT of love, with crooked shutters and light leaking out of every gap in the planks. The back of it opens straight into the forest, so while you stand at the front door you hear the trees behind it as well. Inside it's cozy in a slightly suspicious way: two cups, one blanket, one chair that is clearly NOBODY else's chair. The kettle starts to sing before you even knock.

optionen.name: Look at the two cups
optionen.text: Only one of them has been used. The other is spotless, with a faint ring of dust at the bottom, like it has been waiting a very long time for a guest.

optionen.name: Look out of the back window
optionen.text: Past the black trunks a slope climbs into the fog, and for a moment, high up, there's a single orange glow, small and steady, like an ember somebody forgot. Then the fog moves and it's gone.

varianten.begegnung: The Nook again, and the kettle starts to sing before you even reach the door. Through the window you can see the second cup, and it has been moved closer to the chair you sat in last time. You don't remember telling anyone that you would come back.

ort.see.k1.text: You didn't plan on walking to the lake tonight, your feet just did it, and now there's only black water and fog so thick you see three meters at most. A playground with a rusty swing sits off to the side, and the swing moves a little even though there's no wind. The water makes no sound at all, not one ripple, and THAT is wrong, you know lakes make noise. Somewhere to your left a small red dot glows and fades, glows and fades, like somebody breathing in.

optionen.name: Walk towards the red dot
optionen.text: The fog opens up and a double bench appears next to the playground, with a lazy shape on it, looking out at the water like the water is a TV show and the best part is about to start.

optionen.name: Look at the water
optionen.text: You see your own face, and when you lift a hand your reflection lifts one, half a second late. You decide to blame the fog. You decide that very firmly.

varianten.wiederbesuch: The lake again, the swing again, the red dot gone. The bench is empty now, but the slats are warm, and the fog sits on the water like it's waiting for you to say something.

n1.text: You haven't even knocked when the door flies open and a small guy with messy dark hair and a scarf way too big for him is standing there, cheeks red from the stove. 'Oh. It's you. NOT that I was waiting or anything, I just happened to look out of the window for... the weather, idiot.' His eyes flick to the dark road behind you, back to you, back to the road. 'You're the one moving into Lizzy's house, right? Everyone's been talking.' He stops one sentence too late, like his mouth kept going after the thought was finished. 'Anyway. I made too much tea. It's not like I'm inviting you because I'm lonely or anything.'

wahl.label: Say yes and step inside
wahl.folge: Noah is relieved for a second before he hides it

wahl.label: Ask how he knows who you are
Say you're tired and decline
wahl.folge: Noah's smile freezes for a heartbeat

n2.text: He pushes a cup into your hands, hovers around you, then drops into the one chair that is obviously his and pulls the blanket up over his knees. 'Sit. Not THERE, there's a draft. And don't touch the shelf. Fine, you can touch it, just not the blue box.' He watches you drink, a little too closely, and looks away when you notice. 'I don't have people over. Whatever. It's nice. NOT that it matters to me.' The second cup, clean and dusty at the bottom, stands close to your elbow.

wahl.label: Ask about the second cup
wahl.folge: Noah gets quiet and then tells you

wahl.label: Tell him the tea is good
wahl.folge: Noah goes red and starts talking

n3.text: 'Everybody knows everybody here, idiot, it's a small town.' He crosses his arms, uncrosses them, and his sleeve rides up and you see a stretch of skin on his wrist that is shiny and tight and wrong, like melted candle wax. He yanks the sleeve down. 'Also you drive a car nobody in Lünen would buy, and the post office wouldn't shut up about the letter. So. Don't read into it.' He mutters, quieter, 'Everyone always knows who ends up in that house.' Then the smile snaps back on. 'Tea! Come on, it's getting cold.'

wahl.label: Follow him in for the tea
Let it go and leave
wahl.folge: Noah watches you walk away from the window

n4.text: His smile freezes for exactly one heartbeat. It's not angry, it's EMPTY, like somebody pressed pause on a face, and for that one beat there's nobody behind it at all. Then it's gone and he waves his hand. 'Fine! Whatever! It's not like I care! Go to bed, idiot.' The door is already half shut when he adds, small and fast, 'The house is cold at night. Keep the lights on. All of them.' Then the latch clicks and you hear him humming on the other side, cheerful and tuneless, until it fades.

wahl.label: Go to the house
wahl.folge: The player starts the first night with Noah's warning in mind

n5.text: 'That's for guests.' He grins at the cup instead of at you. 'In case somebody comes. I wash it every morning, it's silly. Nobody has ever used it.' His thumb rubs the rim of his own cup, round and round. 'You're the first one who sat close enough to touch it, if you want to know.' The bright face wobbles around the mouth for a second. 'Go on. You can have it. NOT because I'm sentimental or anything.' He pours with a hand that is not quite steady.

wahl.label: Drink from the second cup
wahl.folge: Noah's trust goes up a lot

wahl.label: Say you don't want to take his guest cup

n6.text: 'DON'T.' It comes out like a slammed door. He's on his feet before you saw him move, one hand on the box, the other flat against your chest, small and hard and shaking, and the blanket lies on the floor. His eyes are huge and dry. Then he blinks and laughs, high and awkward, and takes his hand away like he touched a hot stove. 'I mean! It's just old stuff! Boring! You'd be so bored!' He's breathing too fast. 'Please don't. Okay? I'll make you cookies.'

n7.text: He goes red from the collar to the hairline. 'W-well, obviously it's good, I made it, there's honey in it, and cinnamon, and a SECRET ingredient, so don't ask.' Then it all comes tumbling out, how he built the Nook himself out of scrap wood over three summers, how the stove smokes when the wind comes from the east, how foxes come to the back window at dawn and he leaves them bread. Halfway through a sentence his eyes slide to the window, then to the curtain, like he wants to be sure nobody is looking in. Then the cheerful voice is back as if it had never left.

wahl.label: Ask who he thinks might be looking
wahl.folge: Noah deflects, but it stays in the air

wahl.label: Keep chatting about the foxes
wahl.folge: Noah's trust goes up; he asks you to come back

n8.text: 'Nobody! Nobody is looking, idiot, stop being weird.' He laughs a bit too loudly, takes your cup and washes it right away, hands deep in the basin, shoulders tight. You notice the burnt-wool smell again, very faint, coming off his sweater. 'It's a small town. People look. That's what they do.' He keeps his back to you for a long moment. Then, much softer: 'Just... promise you'll come by again. Okay? Not because I need you to.'

wahl.label: Promise him
wahl.folge: Noah's trust goes up; he smiles for real

wahl.label: Say you'll think about it
wahl.folge: Noah acts like it doesn't hurt

n9.text: The tea is hot and sweet with a faint taste of smoke at the back. Noah watches the cup go up and down with his whole body, leaning forward, and when you set it down empty he lets out a long shaky breath. 'You... drank it. It's been there for four years. Nobody ever...' He presses his sleeve to his eyes. 'Don't look! It's the steam! It's NOT anything!' For a long minute the two of you just sit there, and the only sound is the stove ticking as it cools.

n10.text: You press, and for a second he doesn't react, and then something comes down over his face like a shutter. His shoulders drop, his hands fold in his lap, and his voice is even and very polite. 'Close the box, please.' Not an order. A request, from someone who has never needed to raise his voice to get his way. You close it. He smiles at you a second too long, then blinks, and the bright little guy is back, scratching his neck. 'What? Why are you looking at me like that? Idiot.' Your hand, you notice, is shaking.

wahl.label: Finish your tea and leave
wahl.folge: A seed of the other Noah has been planted

varianten.begegnung: He opens the door before you reach it, again, and this time he doesn't even pretend to look at the weather. 'You're back. That's... fine. I mean, I kept the cup warm. By accident. Because I was walking past the stove. Anyway, get in, idiot.' He hovers a second too long in the doorway, as if checking the road behind you for someone you didn't bring.

n1.text: A man in a washed-out hoodie sits on the double bench with one arm over the backrest and a cigarette burning between two fingers, looking out at the water like it just told him a joke. He doesn't turn his head. 'Evening,' he says, in a voice like warm gravel. 'Funny. I thought you'd come around the other side. Everyone comes around the other side.' The smoke doesn't rise, it just lies down on the fog and joins it. Without looking at you, he holds out a second cigarette, already lit, as if he had known exactly when you'd arrive. 'Welcome gift, man. Wanna smoke?'

wahl.label: Sit down next to him and say no thanks
wahl.folge: Mika's mood stays relaxed and amused

wahl.label: Ask how he knew you were coming
Keep your distance and say hi

n2.text: The slats are cold under you, then, slowly, they turn warm, like the bench was waiting. 'No? Smart,' says Mika, and puts the spare cigarette out on the armrest. 'Good lungs are the first thing to go in this town.' He leans back. 'You're Lizzy's, right? The house. It's got a smell, doesn't it. Don't worry, you stop noticing after the third day. That's the funny part, you stop noticing the fun stuff.' His eyes are calm and red around the rims, and somehow it feels like HE is the one studying you. 'Quick question, man. Left or right around the lake? People always ask me, and I never remember which one was the good one.'

wahl.label: Say left
wahl.folge: Mika smiles a little too wide

wahl.label: Say right
wahl.folge: Mika smiles a little too wide

n3.text: 'Did I? Huh.' He taps ash into the fog, where it just disappears. 'Maybe I didn't. Maybe the bench knew. It's a very old bench, man.' He laughs, a dry little rustle, and finally turns his head. The smile is friendly and lazy and does not reach the part of his face that matters. 'Don't worry about it. Nobody ever gets an answer here. That's what keeps it relaxing.' Behind you the swing stops in the middle of its arc. The offered cigarette is still waiting between his fingers.

wahl.label: Say goodnight and go back
wahl.folge: Mika calls after you: 'See you soon!'

n4.text: 'Respect.' He lifts two fingers in a lazy salute and tucks the spare cigarette behind his ear. 'Boundaries. Smart. Most people forget those.' He looks back at the water and the smoke from his cigarette bends toward it, as if something were pulling. 'If you ever want to talk, I'm usually around. You'll find me. Or I'll find you. The lake is small.' A beat. 'It's SO small, man.'

wahl.label: Walk back to the house
wahl.folge: Mika stays on the bench, still looking at the water

n5.text: 'Ha.' He says it softly, like you handed him a secret. 'Either way. Everybody ends up in the middle anyway.' He flicks the cigarette into the dark and it doesn't make a sound when it lands. The fog tightens around the bench, and for a second you get the feeling that the lake itself has leaned in to listen. 'Go home. Sleep. Come back when you've got questions. I like questions. They're...' he closes his eyes to think, '...nutritious.'

wahl.label: Say goodnight and head back
wahl.folge: The player walks home with a chill on the neck

n6.text: 'That's the right answer.' He looks genuinely pleased, almost fond. 'Staying put. Rare. I like you already.' The ember glows. 'Free secret: the people here are all very nice. Don't trust a single one. Not even the nice ones. ESPECIALLY not the nice ones.' He grins, easy and relaxed. 'See? Free. And hey, if you meet the kid with the scarf, be nice to him. Just be nice.'

wahl.label: Thank him and head home
wahl.folge: Mika's hint level goes up slightly

n7.text: It tastes of clove and tar, and the world goes soft and slow at the edges. The fog breathes in time with your lungs, and for a second the black water has something moving under it, big and unhurried and curious, turning over like a sleeper. 'Easy,' Mika says from far away. 'Easy, man. It passes. Don't look at it too hard. It gets shy.' When you come back, you're hunched on the bench with your pulse in your teeth and the lake is flat again. 'See?' He grins. 'Now you know what it feels like when it looks back.' He pats the slat next to him, and it is already warm.

wahl.label: Sit down next to him
wahl.folge: Mika's hint level goes up slightly

wahl.label: Get up unsteadily and go home
wahl.folge: Mika's hint level goes up slightly

n8.text: He doesn't answer for a while. The ember brightens, dims. 'The kid,' he says at last. 'Hard to be in his skin, man. It's crowded in there.' He taps ash. 'Someday you'll find out why. Not today.' The ember arcs into the dark. 'Go home. And whatever you hear tonight in that house, if the wall gets cold, don't knock on it. It knocks back.'

wahl.label: Walk home through the fog
wahl.folge: Mika has pointed at the wall

varianten.mika_hint: 'Back already,' says Mika, without turning his head. 'I was starting to think you went around the OTHER way.' The ember glows. 'Sit, man. You know the way the bench works now. It sits down with you.' He holds out a lit cigarette without looking. 'Welcome back gift. Wanna smoke?'

n1.text: You can't sleep. The bed is fine, the sheets are fine, YOU are the problem, because the house is not quiet, it is only quiet in the way a person is quiet when they are listening to you listen. Somewhere inside the wall behind the headboard something taps. Tap. Tap. Tap. Pause. It's slow and polite, like a knuckle on a door that doesn't expect an answer. The fog presses against the window. Your phone says 02:41 and no signal.

wahl.label: Pull the blanket over your head
Go and check the warm door at the end of the hall

n2.text: You knock twice with your knuckle, feeling stupid, feeling twelve years old. The tapping stops at once. The silence is so complete you can hear the blood in your ears. Then, exactly where your hand was, from the other side of the plaster, something knocks back, twice, soft and exact, and the wall under your fingers is suddenly so cold it burns. You pull your hand away and it comes back with a faint grey dust on the skin, like chalk, like old ash.

n3.text: You count to a hundred. Then you count backwards, because forwards isn't working. Somewhere around forty-one the tapping starts up again, very quiet, in rhythm with your counting, and you realise it has been counting WITH you the whole time. You stop. It stops. You let out a breath and the room lets out one too, a long slow sigh through the floorboards, like someone sitting back down. You fall asleep, eventually, with all the lights on. When you wake up there's a full cup of tea on the nightstand, steaming, and you don't remember making it.

wahl.label: Get up and start the day

n4.text: The hallway is cold and the floorboards are warm under your bare feet, and neither of those two things should be true at once. The door at the end is open a hand's width now, and breath is coming out of it, warm, damp, slow. Through the gap you can see a circle scratched into the floor, burnt candle stumps standing around it at exact distances like people waiting, and in the middle a dark patch that you decide, without asking yourself, is water damage. A tune is coming from inside, very faint, tuneless, the kind of humming a person does when they are rocking something small.

wahl.label: Close the door and go back to bed

n5.text: You knock three times, hard, to show it who's in charge. The house answers with five. You knock one. It knocks one. You knock four times, very slowly, and from behind the wall, in a clear, bored, child's voice, someone says 'four,' and then, helpfully, 'five,' and then 'six,' the way you'd count out loud to somebody who's hiding. You are already in the hallway with all the lights on before you realise that you ran. The counting goes on behind you, patient, through the plaster, all the way to a hundred, and stops exactly at the number of steps from the bedroom to the front door.

wahl.label: Sleep on the sofa downstairs, lights on

n6.text: The floor in the room is warm like a body. You stand in the doorway of the circle and your toes find the scratches in the boards, and a name is cut into the wood next to your foot, in a cramped hand: LIZZY. And under it, much smaller, scratched over and over until the wood is nearly through: please. The humming has stopped. The door clicks shut behind you, softly, the way you'd close a door on someone you don't want to wake. You count to ten with your hand on the cold wall. On ten the handle gives, as if it had only been holding its breath. In the hallway the clean stripe on the floor leads straight to your feet.

n1.text: The little church is the only lit building on the whole street, and the yellow window pulls you across the cobbles like a moth. Up close it's not glass but a hundred little panes in lead, and each one has a slightly different colour in it, amber, honey, a bruise-purple. Behind the amber pane a man in a dark cardigan is moving chairs. Slowly. One by one. He lifts each chair, sets it down, steps back, tilts his head like a painter, and then moves it half an inch to the left. His lips are moving. You can't hear a word through the glass.

wahl.label: Walk away quietly
wahl.folge: You leave him to his chairs

n2.text: He has stopped moving chairs. Now he's standing in the middle of the nave with his hands folded and he is reading something out loud, a list. You press your forehead to the cold glass and the vibration of his voice comes through the lead in a low murmur, name after name after name. Most of them you don't know. Some sound very old. 'Anneliese,' he says. 'Heinrich. Margarete. Dorothea.' His voice catches on that last one and a long moment goes by. 'Elisabeth,' says the man in the cardigan, very softly. 'Lizzy.'

n3.text: You tap the glass with one knuckle, and the sound is thin and bright and dreadfully loud. The man stops with his hand on a chair back. For a very long moment he doesn't turn. Then his head goes round on his neck, not quickly, calm as a lamp being turned toward a wall, and he looks straight at the amber pane. Straight at you. His eyes are gentle and grey and perfectly empty. He smiles. Then he lifts one finger to his lips, a kind, tired gesture, as if you were a child who'd wandered into a room where somebody was sleeping, and goes back to his chairs.

n4.text: 'Dorothea. Elisabeth. Margarete.' The man in the cardigan reads the list again, from the start, as if saying it a second time would make it come out different. When he reaches the end he stands very still and his shoulders shake once. He takes something from his pocket, small and white, a folded handkerchief maybe, and lays it on the altar next to one single candle, and the candle flame leans, all by itself, toward the amber window, toward you. 'Not yet,' he says, to the empty church, very gently. 'Not yet, my dear. We're so close.' You are halfway down the street before you realise you've stopped breathing.

n1.text: You sit on the crate by the stove because Noah points at it without looking at you, and a second later a cup is in front of you, a blue one with a painted fox, and it is still wet inside. Rinsed-wet, as if it was washed this minute, although you came in ten seconds ago. 'It's just a cup,' says Noah, too fast, dragging the too-big scarf up over his chin, 'I do NOT wash it every morning, idiot, it was drying.' Five other cups on the shelf, all dusty. He pours the honey-cinnamon tea with both hands, tongue between his teeth, and his sleeves hang over his knuckles. On the floor, three steps from the stove, a line of chalk runs across the planks, and he keeps his boots exactly behind it.

n2.text: He stops with the kettle in the air. One plain word, nothing special, and he looks at the stove, the ceiling, the kettle, anywhere else, and his ears go red above the scarf. 'You don't have to say that,' he mutters. 'People say that when they want something.' Then, to the floor: 'Say it again. NOT because I... the first one was too fast, I didn't hear it properly.' His knuckles are white on the handle. He is waiting for it the way you wait for a step in the dark, ready for it not to be there.

n3.text: 'It's a rule,' says Noah, and tucks his boots a little further back, 'it's nothing, it's... idiot, drink your tea.' He pushes the cup an inch toward you, then another inch, a person making sure you can't possibly miss it. 'The stove's good, though. Look at it. I built it from the bricks of the old...' He stops, and his smile goes strange and tidy, like a drawer being closed. 'It's a good stove. That's all it is.' Whatever the chalk is for, it isn't going to be said today, and he is watching your face to see whether you will make it be.

wahl.label: Tell him it's the nicest cup you've ever had

n4.text: You drink. It is far too sweet, with far too much cinnamon, hot enough to burn the roof of your mouth, and you don't care, and across from you Noah watches the level go down with the stillness of somebody watching a bridge hold. When it's empty he takes it before you can set it down, carefully, with both hands, rinses it in the bucket and puts it back on the shelf with the handle turned toward the door, ready for the next time. Then he catches you looking and snaps, 'It doesn't mean anything.' Nobody has ever used that cup, and you both know it.

wahl.label: Leave quietly
wahl.folge: He doesn't say goodbye, but the door stays open

n5.text: 'You're welcome,' says Noah, and says it like a word in another language, carefully, in case it breaks. He tries it again under his breath, 'you're welcome,' then notices you heard and turns his whole body toward the stove. 'Shut up.' You haven't said a thing. He cuts a cookie in two, the bigger half for you, the smaller for himself, then swaps them when he thinks you aren't looking. His hands shake only a little. You drink the tea, and it's too sweet, and you finish it, and he takes the cup with both hands and turns the handle toward the door.

wahl.label: Eat the smaller half
wahl.folge: He notices, and is very quiet

wahl.label: Leave the cup where he can reach it

n1.text: On the path behind the Nook you hear him before you see him, a voice under the trees, flat and careful, like someone reading a line off a card. 'Thank you. Thank you. THANK you. No. Thank you.' Noah is crouched at the edge of the forest in his oversized coat, a heel of bread in his hands, and in front of him a thin red fox sits very still. 'Thank you for having me,' he tries on the fox. 'NOT that I... no.' He grimaces. 'It sounds weird. It always sounds like I'm lying, and I'm not, I just don't know how it's supposed to go.' Behind him, in the bark of the nearest tree, someone has cut small tally marks, seven columns, five to a column, the last one unfinished.

n2.text: He jumps a foot, the fox is gone in one orange streak, and for a moment his hand comes up in front of his face, not to hit, just to cover. Then he sees it's you and the arm comes down, slowly, as if he were embarrassed by it. 'Idiot,' he whispers. 'You scared Marta.' He looks at the bread, at the empty path. 'She only comes if nobody's here. I think. I've never checked.' He pushes the bread into your hand, crumbs on his sleeve. 'You do it. She might come back for you.'

wahl.label: Crouch down and wait with him
Tell him you heard the practising

n3.text: You stay behind the tree. He practises on the fox, then on a stone, then on the empty air where somebody would be standing. 'Thank you for the tea. Thank you for the... for coming.' He stops. It is quiet so long that the fox takes the bread and he just lets her, looking at his hands. 'If somebody ever sits down,' he says, so softly you nearly miss it, 'I'd like to say it right. Once. Without the voice going funny.' He puts his forehead on his knees, and the end of the scarf drags in the dirt.

wahl.label: Step out and sit beside him

n4.text: You sit on the cold ground with him, shoulder almost against shoulder, and hold the bread out on a flat palm. Nothing happens for a very long time. Your knees go numb. Noah's breathing slows to match yours, and in the ferns something rustles, a red nose appears, and Marta takes the bread out of your hand as lightly as a leaf. Beside you Noah makes a sound that isn't a word. 'She never does that,' he whispers. 'Not even for me.' He's smiling with half his face, helplessly, like it was stolen from him. 'Thank you,' he says, to you, and for once it doesn't sound weird at all.

wahl.label: Say nothing and let it stay
Say 'you're welcome, Noah'
wahl.folge: He hides his face in the scarf

n5.text: 'You heard,' he says, and the colour goes up his neck in a flat red wave. He picks at the scarf, at the bread, at the moss. 'Was it bad? Did it sound stupid?' He really wants to know. It's the question of somebody who has never been told the answer, who has had to guess for years whether his voice was the right shape. His shoulders are up around his ears, ready for you to laugh. Marta is back at the edge of the ferns, a red shape in the green, waiting for somebody to put the bread down.

wahl.label: Tell him it sounded stupid, but nice
wahl.folge: He laughs, startled, and then stops, as if it hurt

ort.gymnasium.k2.text: The Gymnasium is a long flat brick building with a dead flag in the damp air and about a hundred windows that all seem to be looking at you. It IS a working school, you can hear a chair scrape and a teacher's patient voice, but the hallways are weirdly clean and weirdly quiet, no shouting, no running, kids walking in pairs with their hands at their sides. By the entrance hang old class photos, row after row, all the way back to the seventies, every frame the same dark wood, every photo with someone in the back row standing a little too far from the others.

optionen.name: Look closely at the class photos
optionen.text: In the older ones there's a small boy in the back row with a scarf up to his chin, in a SUMMER photo, in full sun. In the later ones his face has been scratched out with something sharp, and only in the photos where he is smiling.

optionen.name: Look at the lockers
optionen.text: One locker on the second floor has an N scratched into the metal so deep it tore through the paint, and a strip of tape across the door that says OUT OF SERVICE in a hand you don't recognise.

varianten.wiederbesuch: The Gymnasium again, and the class photos look the same, but the boy in the scarf is standing a little closer to the front row than before. In the second-floor hallway, the locker with the N has had its tape renewed.

ort.haus.k2.text: Daylight doesn't help the house, it only shows you more of it: wallpaper with tiny repeating circles you can't stop seeing once you've noticed them, a cold draft from somewhere inside the walls, and that clean stripe on the floor, fresh again, like somebody swept it during the night. The cup in the kitchen is right side up now and there's something warm in it, tea, you think, though you never made any. The warm door at the end of the hall is open a crack this morning, one finger wide. Rain ticks on the windows.

optionen.name: Drink from the cup
optionen.text: You don't. You pour it out in the sink and it comes out thick and red-brown and smells like old copper, and you tell yourself it was rust from the pipes. It was TOTALLY rust from the pipes.

optionen.name: Peek through the crack in the warm door
optionen.text: A bare room. A circle scratched into the floorboards with burnt candle stumps set around it at exact distances, and in the middle a dark stain you decide to call water damage. The wall facing you is smoother than the others, newer, patched in a hurry. You close the door, and it closes with a soft, almost grateful click.

optionen.name: Search the bedroom drawers
optionen.text: In the bottom drawer there's a church bulletin, brown with age, and on the back a list of names, Lizzy near the top, and one name crossed out so hard that the pen went right through the paper.

varianten.wiederbesuch: The house, again. The cup is full and warm, again, and the crack in the warm door is a little wider than when you left. The wallpaper circles seem to have gotten smaller or you have gotten bigger, you can't say which.

ort.lunuen.k2.text: In daylight Lünen looks even emptier, which you didn't think was possible. Grey sky, a fine drizzle that never quite becomes rain, wet leaves stuck to the pavement, and the bakery is open now, with a bell over the door that rings a second AFTER you've already stepped inside. Two customers and one baker, nobody speaks, they just nod at you like a committee that already voted. A couple walks past arm in arm, same step, eyes straight ahead, not looking at you or at each other. Every shop window has a little handwritten card, same handwriting everywhere, and none of them say what is for sale.

optionen.name: Ask the baker about the man on the lake bench
optionen.text: The baker keeps wiping the same spot on the counter. 'What man?' she says. 'Nobody sits on that bench. Nobody has sat on that bench in years.' She says it very friendly. Her hand keeps wiping, and the spot is already dry.

optionen.name: Ask the baker what she knew about Lizzy
optionen.text: 'Oh, your grandma bought the dark bread, always together with Dorothy, those two were...' She stops. The bell over the door rings, though nobody has come in. 'We don't say that name, dear,' she says, still smiling, and puts a loaf in your hands that you didn't order.

varianten.wiederbesuch: The baker nods the second you step in, as if she had your pastry ready since morning. 'Back so soon, dear.' Nobody else in the shop looks at you, and you notice that their cards in the window have been swapped for new ones.

ort.nook.k2.text: In the rain the Nook looks like a kid's drawing of a house, small and warm and a bit crooked, with smoke curling out of a chimney that really shouldn't be able to hold a fire. Inside, you can see that someone rearranged everything since last night: the chair now faces the door, the second cup has been used, and a plate of cookies waits on the table with a note in round, neat handwriting: DON'T EAT ALL OF THEM. The shelf with the blue box has a cloth over it. Through the back window the forest stands still and dripping, and somewhere between the trees a branch snaps once, like a knuckle.

optionen.name: Eat a cookie
optionen.text: Honey and cinnamon, still warm, honestly the best thing you've eaten in days. When you look up, Noah is watching you with a tiny proud grin that he hides behind his hand the second you notice.

optionen.name: Ask about the cloth on the shelf
optionen.text: 'It's dusty, idiot, leave it,' he says, a bit too fast. Under the cloth you catch the corner of the blue box and the black edge of what looks like a burnt photo frame.

varianten.begegnung: The Nook is warm and the cookie plate is full again, and this time the note on it says DON'T EAT ALL OF THEM, YOU ALWAYS DO. You haven't been here often enough for him to say that. He grins at you from the chair like he's very pleased with himself.

ort.see.k2.text: By day the lake looks like a perfectly normal lake, which is honestly suspicious. Flat grey water under the drizzle, a small gravel beach, the playground with its rusty swing and the double bench by the path... empty. The fog has pulled back a bit, but only a bit, and the far shore keeps appearing and disappearing like somebody is switching it on and off. You notice that no bird makes a sound here, and that every single bench around the lake faces the water. Not one of them faces the town.

optionen.name: Look at the double bench
optionen.text: Empty, but next to it an ashtray is bolted into the ground, full of cigarette butts, every one burned down exactly halfway and put out with a careful twist.

optionen.name: Look at the water
optionen.text: Your reflection is back, and this time it waits for you. It waits a very long time before it lifts a hand, a full second after you did.

varianten.wiederbesuch: The lake again, grey and flat. The ashtray next to the bench has been emptied since your last visit, and the new butts in it are burned down exactly halfway, like the old ones. Your reflection is waiting for you this time before you even lean over.

n1.text: The church is small and plain and smells of candle wax and wet wool, and a man in a dark cardigan is straightening the hymn books on the back pew, lining each one up with the one before it until the edges match like a knife blade. He has gentle grey eyes and the stillness of someone who never has to hurry. 'Ah,' he says, without turning around right away. 'You must be the one from Lizzy's house. Please, don't be startled, I'm Connor. I help look after the community.' He squares the last book and finally smiles, warm and a little sad. 'I do hope the east room isn't too cold for you. It's always been the cold one.'

wahl.label: Ask how he knows which room is cold
Ask about the man on the lake bench
wahl.folge: Connor shows no reaction at all

n2.text: 'Oh, houses like that are always cold in the east room, aren't they?' He laughs, light and easy, and takes the thought out of the air like a book from a shelf. 'Forgive me, friend, it's an old habit. I like to know the people who live near me. We take care of each other here, and of the old houses too, especially the ones with a... history.' He straightens a candle that didn't need it. 'Would you like to come to the supper on Thursday? Nothing formal. Soup, bread, a few friends.'

wahl.label: Say you'd love to
wahl.folge: Connor is pleased, a first small step toward joining

wahl.label: Say maybe, you're still settling in

n3.text: 'Oh, it's a small thing, but a dear one.' His whole face softens. 'We've been here for a long, long time, you see. Longer than the street signs. We look after one another, we remember the old ways, we keep the town in order.' He pats the pew like a friend. 'Most people who come here feel lonely. You'd be surprised how quickly that goes away if you let people in.' It sounds rehearsed, but so kindly that you forgive it.

wahl.label: Say you'd like to know more

n4.text: His hand doesn't slip once on the hymn books. 'The lake? We don't have a man at the lake,' he says, shaking his head pleasantly. 'Perhaps someone from the next village. Or the fog. The fog plays tricks on newcomers.' A pause exactly as long as a breath. 'Do be careful on your walks, won't you? I'd hate for you to catch a cold.' The smile comes back full and bright, like a lamp switched on in a window.

wahl.label: Say you'll be careful
wahl.folge: Connor relaxes, then reminds you about Thursday

wahl.label: Insist that you saw someone
wahl.folge: Connor repeats the same gentle answer, word for word

n5.text: 'Wonderful.' He walks you to the door with a hand that never quite touches your back. The grey light falls on the pews, and each one has a small brass plate with a name on it, all of them but one, whose plate has been unscrewed and left four small clean holes in the dark wood. 'See you soon, friend. Do take care of the house. It's been waiting a very long time for someone like you.'

wahl.label: Leave the church
wahl.folge: The player now knows of the supper on Thursday

n6.text: 'Of course. Whatever feels right.' He nods and doesn't push, which is somehow worse. 'The door is always open, you know. We never close it. People find their way eventually.' He goes back to his hymn books, and as you leave you hear a soft steady sound behind you, one book being squared against another, again and again.

n7.text: For a second his hands stop on the pew. 'Where did you hear that name?' he asks, still gentle, not looking at you. You say it was the baker. 'Ah. Of course.' The candle flame beside him leans away from his breath. 'We do not speak it, friend. It is not a matter of secrecy. It is a matter of respect. She was our dearest, and she left us in a way that still hurts.' He turns and smiles, and the smile is perfect, and for the first time you see how much effort it takes. 'I'd ask you to honour that. Thursday, then?'

varianten.beitritt: Connor is waiting for you on the church steps, and the umbrella in his hand is already open for you. 'Friend, I'm so glad. You came to the supper after all, or so I hear from the others.' He closes his hand around yours, warm and dry. 'Please, come in. The east room, I trust, has been treating you better?'

n1.text: It's raining properly now, and when the door opens, Noah stands there with a towel over his arm, hands wrapped around a steaming mug. 'Oh. You came BACK. That's... fine. I mean, whatever, it's not like I was counting the hours,' he says, and counts them on his fingers behind his back. He pulls you in by the sleeve, drops a towel over your head and rubs your hair, hard and fast. 'You're soaked, idiot. Sit. I made a new batch, honey and cinnamon, so DON'T complain.' The last part comes out small, almost scared, 'Sit down, please,' and then he smiles like it was a joke you were both in on.

wahl.label: Sit down and ask how his week was
Ask about his scarf
wahl.folge: Noah's mood snaps cold for a moment

wahl.label: Ask about the other people in town

n2.text: 'My week? It was fine! Totally normal! I did my... things.' He tucks his feet up and sips. 'I fixed the roof, I read, I tried a new bread recipe and it went wrong and I'm NOT going to talk about it.' He talks fast and bright, the way people talk when they're scared of what comes after a silence. 'The roof still leaks, though. In the corner. I can't reach it properly, it's too high.' A tiny glance at you, then at the ceiling. 'Not that I'm asking for anything.'

wahl.label: Offer to help with the roof
Tell him you like it here

n3.text: His hand is on the scarf before you finish the sentence. For a heartbeat the room goes flat, as if the sound was taken out of it, and he looks at you with a face that is calm and polite and absolutely not his. 'That is not something we talk about.' It's a quiet, even voice, very adult, very cold. Then he blinks, the cheeks go pink, and he swats you with the corner of the blanket. 'I mean, it's cold out, idiot! It's a SCARF! What do you want me to do, freeze?!' He laughs. You laugh too. Neither of you really believes it.

wahl.label: Pretend you didn't notice the change
Say the other voice scared you

n4.text: 'Which ones?' He's looking at his cup. 'Connor's nice. Everyone says Connor's nice. He... brings me soup sometimes.' He says it like a line he memorised. 'And the baker. And the rest. I don't talk to them much. They don't talk to me much either. It's fine, I have the Nook.' Then he looks up and grins like the sun came out. 'And now I have you. Not that it's a big deal.'

wahl.label: Say you're glad to be here
Ask why he doesn't talk to them

n5.text: You end up on the roof in the rain with a hammer, and Noah holds the ladder, rattling off instructions and complaining the whole time, 'No, the OTHER nail, idiot!' When you reach down to hand him a plank, he flinches so hard he nearly lets go of the ladder, one arm up over his head, eyes shut. It lasts half a second. Then he opens his eyes, laughs too loudly and grabs the plank. 'Sorry! Slipped! I'm clumsy!' You both know that wasn't a slip. By the time the roof stops dripping you're drenched, and he's talking about nothing, very fast, to cover the quiet.

wahl.label: Say nothing and finish the roof

n6.text: By the time you stand up to leave, the rain has turned to a thin grey drip, and he has somehow fed you three cookies and a second cup of tea. At the door he catches your sleeve with two fingers and lets go again quickly. 'Come again. Tomorrow, maybe. Or not tomorrow. Whenever. I'm usually here.' You are halfway down the road when you think you hear him say, very quietly, to the empty room behind him, 'Please don't.'

wahl.label: Walk home
wahl.folge: Noah's lines will carry more doubt next time

n7.text: He looks at you for a long, flat moment, and the cheerful boy isn't home. 'Nobody,' he says, with absolute calm. 'Nobody ever did anything to me. It's rude to say that.' Then the lights come back in his eyes, wet and bright, and his mouth wobbles. 'Please, don't. I like you. I'd like to keep liking you. Please can we just have tea?' Both his hands are shaking in his lap, and he has stopped breathing.

wahl.label: Take his hand
wahl.folge: Noah breaks down for a second, then recovers

varianten.begegnung: He doesn't bother with the towel this time, he just stands aside and lets you in, with a small nervous shrug. 'You came back AGAIN. I mean, obviously you did, because there are cookies, but still.' His eyes flick over your face, searching for something, and relax. 'You didn't talk to him, did you? Never mind. Forget it. Sit.'

n1.text: Connor stands in front of a classroom door with a stack of workbooks, as calm in the middle of a hallway full of kids as he was in the church. They flow past him in pairs and every single one nods at him, a quick respectful dip of the chin, almost a bow. 'Ah, our new neighbour. Do come in, friend.' He opens the door onto a small room with a crucifix, a globe, and a shelf of books whose spines all face exactly the same way. 'I teach religion and ethics here. I also keep the keys, the bell and the coffee, which is the only real power in a school.' He winks.

wahl.label: Ask how long he has worked here
wahl.folge: Connor tells a story that is slightly too perfect

wahl.label: Ask about the old class photos
Ask if he knows Noah
wahl.folge: Connor smiles a fraction too gently

n2.text: 'Thirty-one years, if you can believe it. Since before most of these children's parents were born.' He sets the workbooks down. 'You see, a town like this isn't made of buildings. It's made of habits, the right ones, passed from person to person. I like to think of myself as a gardener of habits.' He lets that hang, pleased with it. 'Thursday, the supper. You will come, won't you? It's the best way to meet everyone at once.'

n3.text: The calm doesn't change, but something behind it does, the way a pond changes when a fish turns underneath. 'Old photographs. Yes. They collect like dust, don't they.' He lines a pencil up with the edge of his desk. 'Some faces haven't aged well in them. We tried to tidy up. I would rather not speak about people who were hurt by their own memories.' Then, pleasantly: 'Have you met anyone in particular?'

n4.text: 'Noah.' He says the name the way you carry a very fragile cup. 'Dear boy. We all look out for him. He's had a hard life, and he's so very sensitive.' Connor's gentle eyes rest on you and weigh you like a loaf of bread. 'He seems to like you. That is good. I only ask that you be kind to him. And that you tell me if he ever seems... unwell.' It's a kind request. It also sounds like a task.

wahl.label: Say you'll look out for him
wahl.folge: Connor trusts you a bit more, and so does the trap

wahl.label: Say Noah is fine on his own
wahl.folge: Connor smiles and lets it go

n5.text: The bell rings and a hundred doors open at once. Kids flood the hall in silent pairs, hands at their sides. Connor lays a hand lightly on your shoulder, just for a second. 'Thursday,' he says. 'Don't be late.' Then he is gone down the corridor, straightening a picture frame as he passes.

wahl.label: Leave the school
wahl.folge: The player is now clearly on Connor's radar

varianten.beitritt: Connor is expecting you. A second chair is already pulled up to the desk. 'Our friend from the supper,' he says warmly. 'It's wonderful to see you again. People spoke of you for days.' He pours a cup of coffee you didn't ask for, and it's exactly how you take it, which you have never told anyone in this town.

n1.text: The bell rings a second after you step in, and the smell is so good it makes you angry: yeast, butter, cinnamon, hot sugar. The baker, a round woman with floury forearms, beams at you across the counter like you're the first customer in a year. Behind the glass there are rows and rows of rolls, all identical, golden and perfectly spaced. 'The new one!' she says. 'From Lizzy's house! What can I get you, dear? Dark bread? Your grandma loved the dark bread.' She's already wrapping a loaf in paper. She didn't ask if you wanted it.

wahl.label: Take the bread and ask about the man on the lake bench
Ask about the boy at the Nook

n2.text: 'What man?' The knife doesn't stop moving. She cuts a fresh roll in half, and in half again, and in half again, until there's nothing left to cut but crumbs. 'There's nobody at the lake, dear. There hasn't been anybody on that bench for... oh, you don't want to know how long. People sit there sometimes, in the fog, but it's the fog, isn't it. It makes shapes.' She pushes a paper bag of crumbs across the counter with a bright smile. 'For the ducks. Will that be all?'

wahl.label: Ask about the boy at the Nook

n3.text: 'Oh, Noah.' The whole shop seems to lean toward the name. 'Poor lamb. He comes every Tuesday for the day-old bread, and he says thank you three times, and he never looks me in the eye.' She lowers her voice, though there's nobody else in the shop. 'His parents used to run this place, you know. Before.' She stops herself. 'Before they went away. Connor looks after him now. Connor looks after everyone.' She presses a warm roll into your hand. 'Take this to him, would you? Tell him it's from me. He won't take it from me, he's too proud. He'll take it from you.'

wahl.label: Take the roll for Noah
wahl.folge: You carry a warm roll to the Nook

n1.text: From the fence the schoolyard looks like a photograph of one: fifteen kids in grey sweaters, all standing in a circle, all facing inward, all absolutely still. In the middle of the circle one smaller kid stands with his arms stiff at his sides and his eyes squeezed shut. Nobody speaks. A teacher at the far wall checks her watch. After what feels like a full minute, a girl at the edge of the circle says, very softly, 'One,' and the whole circle takes one step in. Nobody laughs. Nobody pushes. The kid in the middle doesn't move at all.

wahl.label: Ask the teacher what the game is

n2.text: 'Oh, that? It's called The Keeper.' The teacher is young, tired, and smiles without using her eyes. 'They made it up themselves. Somebody has to be the Keeper and stand in the middle and not move, no matter what, and the others come closer, a step every time they say the next number. If the Keeper moves, they all have to start again.' She looks at the circle. 'Nobody's ever moved, though. Not once. I've been here six years.' She shivers a little and laughs at herself. 'They say it's very peaceful, being in the middle.'

n3.text: They count to twelve. By then the circle has shrunk until the children stand shoulder to shoulder around the small boy, so close that they're touching his sleeves. 'Twelve,' says the girl. The Keeper opens his eyes. They are huge and calm and a very pale grey, and he smiles at all of them, one by one, and says in a clear, unbothered voice: 'Thank you for keeping me.' The circle breaks with a roar of ordinary laughter, kids shoving and shouting, all of them suddenly children again, and the boy who was the Keeper runs to the swings without looking back.

n4.text: A girl with a black braid waves you over to the fence and looks you up and down very seriously. 'You can be the Keeper,' she says. 'Grown-ups are always good at it, they're so used to standing still.' The circle opens for you like a mouth. You stand in the middle, arms down, eyes shut, as the voices start to count. 'One.' Feet on gravel. 'Two.' The cold breath of fifteen children. 'Three.' Someone's fingers touch your sleeve, so lightly you could be imagining it. By 'seven' you can feel them all pressing in, a ring of warmth and small breaths. By 'eleven' you realise nobody is holding you, and also that you couldn't move if you tried. 'Twelve,' says the girl with the braid, and then, close to your ear, tenderly: 'You're very good at this.'

n1.text: The attic stairs are hidden behind a panel in the upstairs hall, and the panel isn't locked, which is worse. Up there the air is dry and golden with dust, and the roof beams are so low you have to duck. Boxes. Hat boxes, shoe boxes, a dressmaker's dummy with a sheet over its head like a patient waiting for a diagnosis. In the far corner under the round window stands a wooden trunk with LIZZY burned into the lid, and next to it, on the floor, a very old black-and-white photograph has been placed face up, as if somebody had been looking at it a moment ago.

wahl.label: Look under the sheet on the dummy

n2.text: It's the same photograph as the one in the kitchen tin, but this one has writing on the back, a faded pencil list. Five names, one for each person standing in front of the house: Lizzy. Hans. Margarete. Dorothea. And a name that has been scratched out with a blade so deep the paper is torn. You hold the photograph up to the round window. The woman in the middle, Lizzy, is not looking at the camera. She's looking at the person at the far right of the frame, the one whose name was scratched out, and on her face there's an expression you've seen on women at funerals: grief, and under the grief, something much quieter and much worse: relief.

n3.text: The lid is heavy and the hinges give a sound like a held-in scream. Inside there's lavender, dried to dust, and under it, folded in tissue paper, a child's winter coat, tiny, grey wool, the kind with a hood. At the bottom, loose, a single red mitten, hand-knitted, scorched along one edge. The other one is missing. When you pick it up, you notice that someone has stitched a letter into the cuff, in black thread: a clumsy, careful N. You don't know why your hands are shaking. You put it in your pocket anyway, because leaving it here feels like leaving a child in the dark.

wahl.label: Go back downstairs
wahl.folge: You leave the attic with the mitten

n4.text: The sheet slides off into your hand with a dry whisper. The dummy underneath has no head, of course. But somebody has drawn a face on the canvas neck with a pencil: two eyes, a mouth, tiny and neat. And around the neck, hanging from a nail, is a small iron key on a red cord, exactly like the one Connor wears. Under the key there's a note pinned to the cloth in the round, careful handwriting you saw on the Nook door: THE ONE WHO COMES BACK WILL WANT THIS. DON'T GIVE IT TO HIM. The 'him' has been underlined three times. You don't take the key. You can feel the dummy watching you with its pencil eyes anyway, all the way down the stairs.

n1.text: You find the paper while fetching the kettle, a page torn from a school notebook and pinned under the sugar tin, with a title he went over three times: WHEN I WOKE UP. Under it, a tidy list, a date on every line. Kettle still warm, nobody here. Mud on the boots, dry. Smoke on both sleeves. The last line has no date yet, only a pencil stub waiting. You haven't read it twice when his hand slaps down over the page, fast, his face gone white. 'That's NOT for you,' says Noah, too loud. 'It's a shopping list.'

wahl.label: Hand it over and say nothing
Tell him the truth: you read it
Say it's none of your business anyway

n2.text: He crumples the page against his chest and stands there breathing like somebody who has run a long way. 'Thanks,' he says, and it cracks. Then he smooths it flat on the table instead, very gently. 'I started it so I'd be able to tell somebody. If something happened.' He doesn't look up. 'Sometimes the day has a hole in it. That's all. Everybody has that, probably.' A laugh with no air in it. 'It's just that mine has smoke in it.' His cuff has ridden up and he pulls it down over his hand, not fast, almost politely.

wahl.label: Ask if he wants to add a line

n3.text: 'Okay,' says Noah, very small. The page doesn't move under his hand. The stove ticks. 'Then you know.' He doesn't say what. 'I don't hurt anybody,' he says, low and quick, 'I check, every time, I walk down to the road and I look and it's always fine, it's always...' His eyes come up to yours, very wide, very pale. 'You'd tell me, right? If it wasn't. You wouldn't pretend.'

n4.text: He holds the pencil out to you, which you did not expect. 'You write it,' he says. 'Today. If there's a hole today, you write what happened, and then I'll know. NOT because I... don't make it a thing.' The pencil is bitten flat at the end. You write the date, and under it, in your own loud handwriting: Noah made tea. Fox came. Nothing else. He reads it twice with his lips moving, then folds the page into a very small square and puts it in the pocket over his heart.

wahl.label: Say nothing and pour the tea
wahl.folge: The page stays in his pocket

n5.text: 'Everybody,' he says, trying it out, 'forgets things.' He sounds like he would like to believe it badly enough to sign something. He sits on the other crate with the page on his knee, and rubs his wrist, and you see the edge of something smooth and shiny and old before he catches it and pulls the cuff down. 'Don't,' he says, nearly politely. 'I'll make the tea.' His hands are steady on the kettle, so steady, a person's hands who has practised being steady. On the last line of the page he writes: tomorrow, check the road. It is the first line with a tomorrow in it.

wahl.label: Hold the cup for him
wahl.folge: He lets you, which costs him something

n6.text: 'Promise,' he repeats, and the word sits in him like a warm stone. He has been given very few. He smooths the page and, on the empty last line, in capitals, writes: IF I DON'T KNOW, THEY WILL TELL ME. Then, smaller, below: they. He glances at you to check you didn't read it, and looks at the stove. 'You can't take it back now. That's the rule.' It sounds exactly like a child making up a rule on the spot so a good thing can't be taken away.

wahl.label: 'I know the rule.'
wahl.folge: He keeps the page against his heart

n7.text: 'Right.' Noah folds the page in half, and in half again, and slides it into the sugar tin, and puts the lid on. 'Sorry. It's not interesting.' He pours the tea and the tea is the right temperature and the cup is the right cup and he asks nothing, says nothing, and talks about the weather as if it were an exam. You drink. It is, for a while, just a hut with a boy in it who is being perfectly polite. When you leave he holds the door and says 'bye' in a voice so even that you could lay a ruler along it.

wahl.label: Leave
wahl.folge: He closes the door and stands behind it

n1.text: At the lake the fog lies so low that the water seems to have been taken out and only the sound of it left. Noah is on the old jetty in his socks, his boots lined up beside him, a flat stone in his hand he hasn't thrown, and you see his bare forearms for the first time because he has rolled his sleeves up to wash. The skin is shiny and pulled and mottled, healed long ago, more memory than skin. He sees you and doesn't pull the sleeves down. He freezes with the stone. 'It's NOT a thing,' he says. 'Just don't stand so close to the water. Okay? The planks are old.'

wahl.label: Stay on the shore and nod
Walk onto the jetty beside him

n2.text: You stay on the shore. He hasn't moved the sleeves, and it's costing him, he is holding still the way you hold still for a doctor. 'Water's okay,' he says, to the lake. 'It's the other thing I can't. Near the fire everything goes, and then it's a different day.' He rolls the stone in his palm. 'There's someone who says it's good to look at them. The scars. He says it keeps me honest.' His neck jerks, once, at his own sentence. 'Don't tell him I said that. Don't tell anybody. NOT that there's anyone.'

wahl.label: Offer to skip the stone instead

n3.text:
{{KRACK!}}

The plank gives under your heel, not all the way, just enough that your leg drops through to the ankle in the icy water, and before you can yell Noah's hand has your sleeve, hard, dragging you back, his whole thin body leaning against your weight. He's shaking. He's much stronger than he looks. 'Idiot, idiot, I SAID, the planks...' His voice comes out high and cracked. He lets go at once, as though you burned him, and looks at the red print of his fingers on your coat. 'Did I hurt you? Tell me if I hurt you.'

n4.text: He stands very still, as if the words had to settle on him like snow. Then slowly he lowers his sleeves, one, then the other, buttoning the cuffs, and you realise he wasn't hiding them from you any more, he was giving them to you, and now he's taking them back because the afternoon is over. 'My boots are cold,' he says in a voice that is almost laughing. He sits on the planks, and after a moment you sit beside him, a safe distance from the water. 'Do you want to throw it? I never got the hang of it. It always sinks.'

wahl.label: Throw it
wahl.folge: It sinks, with a lot of dignity

wahl.label: Tell him it's your first time too

n5.text: He puts the stone in your hand, flat and cold and smooth, with a little warmth from his palm still in it, and watches you throw. It sinks at once. It sinks like a stone. He makes a sound you've never heard from him, short, undignified, a snort. 'That was awful. That was the worst I've ever seen.' He's laughing, the ugly honest kind that folds a person in half, arms round his stomach, the scarf coming loose. When he can breathe he wipes his eyes, and his face is open and very young. 'Do it again,' he says. 'Please. Tomorrow, too, if you... NOT that I'm asking.'

wahl.label: Throw another
wahl.folge: He counts the skips out loud

wahl.label: Tell him you'll be here tomorrow

ort.gymnasium.k3.text: After class hours the Gymnasium is a different building, and you feel it the moment you step in. The hallway echoes, the clock over the exit ticks too loudly, and every classroom is cleaned to the point of sterility with all the chairs on the desks. The only light on is in the office at the end, where Connor's silhouette moves behind frosted glass, humming a hymn so slowly you need a moment to recognise it. On the wall by the stairs the photos have been replaced again: the ones with the scratched-out boy are gone, and in the new frames there is nobody in the back row at all.

optionen.name: Look into the empty classroom
optionen.text: On the board, in neat chalk, a half-erased list of names in two columns, STAYED and LEFT. One name in the second column was wiped so thoroughly that the board is almost white there.

optionen.name: Knock on Connor's office door
optionen.text: The humming stops. 'One moment, friend.' The door opens exactly as far as his face, and he is smiling, though behind him the office is perfectly dark. 'Is something the matter? You're up late.'

varianten.beitritt: Connor's office door is open this time, and a chair stands ready by the desk. 'Friend,' his voice says from inside, 'you've been to our table, so you may as well come in and sit.' The hallway photos have all been replaced, but there is one new frame by the stairs, and in the back row of it, smiling, stands somebody who looks very much like you.

ort.haus.k3.text: The house has started to feel like it knows you. The floor stripe is there every morning, the kitchen cup is always warm, and the warm door at the end of the hall is open a hand's width now, not a finger. You've caught yourself standing in front of it for minutes, listening. It doesn't breathe, exactly. It WAITS. Out of the bedroom window you see, for the third night in a row, a small figure under the lamp across the road, looking up at the house, wrapped in a scarf that is too big for him. When it starts to rain he doesn't move.

optionen.name: Go to the window and look down
optionen.text: The figure is gone by the time you reach the glass, but the street lamp is flickering, and in the wet leaves at the curb there's one clean footprint, small, pointing at your front door.

optionen.name: Step into the warm room
optionen.text: You get one foot over the threshold. The air is thick and sweet like syrup, and the patched wall hums faintly like a hive. You back out and close the door with shaking hands, and the humming stops the second the latch clicks.

varianten.wiederbesuch: You come home to the house, and the hallway smell is a little sweeter, a little closer, like you've been breathing it all day. The warm door is open a hand's width, and tonight you notice you've left your shoes in front of it, like at a church.

ort.lunuen.k3.text: Thursday has come and gone, and the town feels different in a way you can't quite name. There are more people on the street now, maybe four instead of two, and they all walk in the same direction, toward the church, none of them hurrying, rain dripping from their umbrellas. Somebody pinned black ribbons on the bakery door, and the baker greets you now with your name, which you don't remember telling her. Everyone smiles at you. It's very pleasant. You count the smiles, and they're all exactly the same width.

optionen.name: Ask why the ribbons are on the door
optionen.text: 'For the anniversary,' the baker says gently. 'We hold a little remembrance every year, for an old friend. Everyone is welcome, of course.' She presses a pastry into your hand. It's warm, and it's exactly the pastry you like, which is creepy.

optionen.name: Follow the crowd for a moment
optionen.text: You walk behind them for a block. Nobody speaks. At the church door every one of them touches the wood with two fingers, and there's a slightly darker patch, worn smooth by decades of the same small gesture.

varianten.wiederbesuch: The town is busier than it was this morning, and the crowd has moved a little: four people at the church door, then six, then a line. The baker waves at you from the window, but she doesn't come out. Her smile is the same width as before.

ort.nook.k3.text: The Nook's door is open and the stove is cold, which you know is wrong, because it's NEVER cold. The cups are washed and stacked, the blanket is folded in a neat square, and the cloth that used to cover the blue box lies in a corner. On the table is a note in that round, careful handwriting: GONE FOR WOOD. BACK SOON. DON'T WORRY. The last three words are underlined twice, hard enough to dent the paper. Through the back window the path into the trees looks darker than before, and the dishes in the sink are still wet.

optionen.name: Open the blue box
optionen.text: Inside there's no photo frame, only ash, packed into the corners like it was put there on purpose, and a little silver locket on a broken chain with nothing in it.

optionen.name: Wait for Noah
optionen.text: You wait twenty minutes. He doesn't come. When you finally leave, the door swings shut behind you by itself, and from somewhere outside you hear light quick footsteps running away through the leaves.

varianten.begegnung: The Nook is still empty, the stove still cold. Your own handwriting is on the table now, the note you left last time, and under it Noah's reply in neat round letters: I SAW. THANK YOU FOR COMING. DON'T LOOK FOR ME IN THE FOREST. The last sentence is underlined twice.

ort.see.k3.text: Dusk, and the fog has crept back to the shore, a flat white wall, and walking the shore path feels like walking along the inside of a bottle. The rain sits on the water in tiny rings that never overlap. The double bench is empty, but when you put your hand on the seat, it's warm, as warm as if somebody had just stood up. In the wet sand run two sets of footprints toward the water, one pair of shoes, one pair of bare feet. Only one set comes back. For the first time since you got here the lake makes a sound, a small wet lap at the end of the second trail.

optionen.name: Follow the bare footprints to the water
optionen.text: They end right at the waterline. You crouch. Below the surface, under the moving fog, a pale shape that might be a hand opens and closes once, like someone waving from a long way down.

optionen.name: Sit on the warm bench
optionen.text: The warmth soaks into you like a hug. A voice that sounds like it's right next to your ear says, 'Good. Stay a while.' Nobody is there.

varianten.mika_hint: The bare footprints have been joined by a second set, yours, you realise, though you haven't walked here yet today. They stop at the waterline. In the fog above the surface a vaguely human shape is sitting very still, and it is smoking.

ort.wald.k3.text: The forest begins right behind the Nook, and it doesn't ease you in: one step and the road noise is gone, two steps and even the rain sounds different, dripping slowly from huge dark trees that stand much too close together. Every trunk has a scratched circle at hip height with three dots inside. A narrow path climbs away to the right, up toward a ridge you can't see, and at the edge of the dusk you can make out a black patch of ground where nothing has ever grown back. Behind you, softly, a twig snaps. You stop. It stops.

optionen.name: Take the path up the slope
optionen.text: Halfway up the ground turns black underfoot, a wide scorched patch without grass or moss, ash worked into the soil like dirty snow. Whatever burned here burned for a very long time, and somebody has raked the ashes smooth since.

optionen.name: Look at the scratched circles
optionen.text: You know this sign. A circle with three dots in it. You saw it scratched into the floorboards of the warm room in your house, and it has the same careless, practiced hand.

optionen.name: Listen to the twig snapping behind you
optionen.text: You turn around. Nothing. Only wet trees and a very quiet gap between two trunks, where someone has been standing a moment ago.

varianten.wiederbesuch: The forest has the same twig-snap and the same dripping dark, but the red thread hasn't been strung yet, and the scorched patch looks very slightly larger than before. The ash is raked again, in fresh clean lines, though no one has passed you on the path.

k3.noah_verfolgt.text: You've been hearing it for twenty minutes now, small footsteps a bit behind you in the rain, stopping when you stop, speeding up when you speed up, the way a kid follows a stranger and thinks he's being sneaky. You whip around, and the forest turns with you, nothing but wet black trunks, and a long pale scarf end that slips behind a tree a second too late. You say his name just to be sure, and the forest goes completely silent. Then, softer than you'd expect, you hear him breathe in and out on the other side of that trunk, and a sound that could be a laugh or a sob. When you walk around the tree, nobody's there. Only, on a stump, a mug of tea, still steaming, set neatly in the rain.

n1.text: The supper was warm. That's the first thing you'll admit about it, later, to yourself. The long wooden table, the bread, the soup that tasted like your childhood, thirty people saying grace like one voice. Now it's over, and Connor walks you out into the dark church yard, hands in his sleeves, breath white in the rain. 'You did very well tonight, friend. People noticed. They like you. That's rare.' He looks up at the dripping sky. 'I would like to ask you something. No pressure. You've come to a hard place, to a house that carries a lot of weight. We could help you carry it. Together.'

wahl.label: Ask what he means by weight
Say you'll think about it
wahl.folge: Connor smiles and lets it rest

wahl.label: Say you don't need help
wahl.folge: Connor accepts, with a flicker of disappointment

n2.text: 'Houses remember,' he says simply. 'Yours has remembered for a hundred years. It remembers who lived in it and what they asked of it.' He turns his hands palm up as if holding something delicate. 'Your great-grandmother, if we're being exact, the letter says grandmother but that's the lawyers, was one of those who understood. She was loved here. She trusted us with her work. I think she'd have wanted you to know us.'

n3.text: 'Of course. Take the time you need.' He smiles like a lantern in a window. 'We're patient. It's the one thing this town does better than anywhere else.' He squeezes your arm and lets go. 'Come to the lake on Sunday morning, before the fog. We meet there. Just to watch. No obligations.'

wahl.label: Nod and walk home
wahl.folge: Connor will push again at the lake

n4.text: For a moment his face doesn't move at all. Then it softens again, a mask put back on its hook. 'Of course. I understand perfectly.' He nods as if filing something away. 'If you change your mind. And do be careful in the forest. It's so easy to lose your way there. And the young man who follows you will not always follow so politely.' He says it kindly, the way you'd say it's going to rain.

wahl.label: Ask what he means about the young man
Walk away
wahl.folge: Connor has told you that he knows about Noah following you

n5.text: 'Only that you aren't the first he has befriended,' says Connor gently. 'And that it would be a kindness to be careful with him. He is very fragile, and fragile things, my friend, have a way of breaking at the worst moment.' He lets the word 'break' hang a heartbeat longer than the others. 'Good night. Thank you for coming. It means more than you know.'

wahl.label: Walk home through the rain
wahl.folge: The player has doubts about both Connor and Noah

varianten.beitritt: Connor waits for you at the church door after the supper, and he is smiling like a man who has already heard the answer. 'You came back to the table. Twice now. That says more than words, friend.' He draws a small iron key out from his collar for a second, shows it, and tucks it away. 'There's something I'd like to ask you at the lake on Sunday. But I think you already know what.'

n1.text: You find him where the forest meets the shore, sitting on a tree stump like it's a throne, smoking and watching the water through a gap in the trees, the rain dripping off his hood like it doesn't bother him. 'Hey,' he says, not surprised. 'Long way from the bench. You're getting brave.' He pats the other stump, which didn't exist a second ago. 'So. You've been to the hill, huh? The black spot. Smells like old fires. Don't worry, that's just history. History's always on fire somewhere.' He glances sideways at you, grinning lazily. 'Did the kid follow you? He does that. Good kid. Hard to be in his skin.'

wahl.label: Ask how he knows about the kid
Ask what happened on the hill

n2.text: 'I know everything that happens around here, man. It's a small place. Everybody ends up on my bench sooner or later.' He blows out smoke and it curls around his head like a halo. 'Look. I like you. So here's one for free: you don't know who anybody is yet. That's not an insult, it's just true. Connor's not who he looks like. The kid's not. The nice people are the worst.' He taps ash. 'And me? I'm just the guy on the bench.'

wahl.label: Ask what he means about Connor
Say thanks and leave
wahl.folge: Mika calls out 'Left or right, remember!'

n3.text: 'Fire.' He says it softly, like the name of a pet. 'A long time ago they put a kid on that hill and lit the wood. That's the whole story. They wanted somebody back. Somebody didn't come back. Something else did.' His eyes stay on the water. 'It's a boring story, honestly. Nothing you can do about it. But people ask, so.' For half a second his grin has too many corners. 'Anyway. Wanna smoke?'

wahl.label: Say yes
wahl.folge: Mika's laugh is a bit too long

n4.text: 'Me? I told you. The guy on the bench.' He laughs, and the laugh carries across the water and comes back from the far shore half a second late. 'Okay, okay. Look, man, I'm nobody. I'm what's left when everybody else has gone home. The one who watches.' You notice that his shadow lies the wrong way, pointing at the lake. 'Go on. Ask your next question. They get better.'

wahl.label: Ask what happened on the hill

n5.text: 'Smart.' He laughs. 'Not many say no. I'll remember that.' He flicks the butt into the fog. 'Go home. The forest isn't fun after dusk. And, hey.' He looks at you for real now, and the lazy eyes are suddenly very, very clear. 'Whatever you do, do NOT go into the cellar of the castle. Absolutely not. It's so boring down there.' He winks.

wahl.label: Walk back
wahl.folge: Mika has just pointed straight at the cellar

n6.text: The smoke tastes of cloves and pond water and something sweet underneath. Your head goes loose and warm, and for a minute the fog by the stump looks like faces, calm, curious, a hundred of them, all looking at you without eyes. 'Easy,' says Mika from far away. 'Easy. It passes.' You come back to yourself sitting on the stump, shaking, mouth dry. 'There,' he says kindly. 'Now you know what it feels like when it looks back.'

wahl.label: Thank him and head home, dizzy

varianten.mika_hint: 'Oh. You,' says Mika, and for once he sits up straight. 'You smell like the church. Not good. Not terrible.' He wrinkles his nose, then laughs. 'Relax, man, I'm kidding. Mostly. But if you keep eating their soup, you'll start humming their hymns. And I don't think you want that. I really don't.'

n1.text: The path forks, and you take the right fork for no reason, and fifty meters on the trees simply stop. The clearing is perfectly round. The grass in it is too short, as if it had been cut with scissors, and in the middle stands a ring of old stones about knee-high, each one carved with the same sign: a circle, three dots. Outside the ring the forest is dripping and loud; inside there's no sound at all. A single candle burns on the biggest stone, not a stub but a fresh white one, with a tiny steady flame that doesn't move in the wind.

wahl.label: Look at the trees around the clearing

n2.text: The moment your foot crosses the line of stones, your ears pop, like going down a mountain road. Inside the ring the air is warm, almost sweet, and the ground under the short grass is crumbly black. Ash. You're standing on top of something enormous that burned a very long time ago and has never fully gone out. You crouch and scoop up a handful of the dark soil. It's warm in your palm, like skin, like a living thing's back, and for a heartbeat you hear it: a thin, high crackling under your fingers, and under the crackling something small and far away that might be a child, breathing in sharp, short sobs.

wahl.label: Drop the ash and step out
Press your ear to the ground

n3.text: You bend down and blow, and the flame goes out. Instantly the clearing fills with sound: wind, rain, a bird, your own breath. You straighten up, proud of yourself, and the candle on the stone behind you lights itself with a soft cough. When you turn around it's burning again, tiny and steady, exactly as before, but the wick is a little shorter. You understand that you didn't win anything. You've only used up a bit of somebody else's patience.

wahl.label: Leave the clearing
wahl.folge: You walk back to the path
