n4.text: Every tree around the clearing has a rope tied to a branch at head height, and every rope ends in a little cloth doll, a hundred of them maybe, hanging perfectly still. They've been here for a very long time. The cloth is grey and green with moss, and the button eyes are filled with rain. They all face the stones. They all face the candle. And one, the nearest, small and red-and-white, hangs a little lower than the others, a recent one, with a scrap of wool scarf tied around its neck.

wahl.label: Leave the clearing
wahl.folge: You walk back to the path

n5.text: You scrape the ash off your palm, and it falls in a neat thin line, and the line points back up the path, toward the hill. You walk out of the ring without looking back. At the edge of the clearing, where the grass becomes ordinary again, there's a small clear footprint in the mud, pointing toward you, as if somebody had stood there for a long time, watching you do all this. It's the size of a child's shoe, or a small man's. The scarf thread on the nearest branch is still swinging.

n6.text: The ground is hot against your cheek, and the crackling gets clearer: not fire. Voices. A circle of voices singing a hymn so slow it takes you a whole verse to recognise it as the tune Connor hummed in the church. Beneath it, higher, thinner, a small voice is saying a single word over and over, in a rhythm like a heartbeat: 'Mama. Mama. Mama.' Then the singing stops, all at once, and there's the sound of wood settling, and a silence that goes on and on, and from very far down comes the sweetest, most patient sentence you have ever heard: 'It worked. Look. It worked.' You tear your head up from the ground with your ears ringing and your cheek covered in warm ash.

n1.text: The Nook is empty and the door isn't locked, because Noah has never locked a door in his life. Wet footprints lead out through the back, toward the trees. You tell yourself you're only here to leave the warm roll on the table. But the floor creaks in one spot by the chair, a little higher than the rest, and the plank is cut cleanly along one edge. Someone has lifted it many times. Under it you can feel cold air coming up.

wahl.label: Look through the drawing book first

n2.text: Under the board there's a biscuit tin like the one in Lizzy's kitchen, and a school exercise book with a red cover, softened by years of handling. Inside the tin are a dozen candle stubs, a little silver locket with no picture, and a stack of folded notes in the same careful, round handwriting as the sign on the door. They're all lists, dated and numbered, and every list has the same title: WHEN I WOKE UP. 'Kettle warm. Mud on my boots. Door open. Smell of smoke on my sleeves.' 'Kettle warm. Paper cut on my thumb that I don't remember. A tooth I don't know in my pocket.' You close the tin before you can read the last list. Your hands are cold as stones.

n3.text: The book is the one with the children's drawings. You've seen the last pages, the big dark building and the small boy in the scarf. But the middle pages you haven't. One shows a very tall figure in a doorway, drawn in thick black crayon, and underneath, in an adult hand, THIS IS NOT YOU. The next shows the same figure holding a smaller figure by the neck, held up off the ground, and the small one is crossed out with so much pressure the page is nearly torn through. The one after is blank, except for a single word, written over and over in a child's loopy hand until the whole page is black: sorry.

n4.text: It's a diary, kept like a prisoner's calendar: dates, little tallies, one line per day. Most days say 'good' or 'ok' or 'tea, cookies, quiet.' Some days say nothing at all, just a blank, and the next day: 'lost a day again.' The last page is from yesterday. 'Somebody sat on the floor and drank from the guest cup. I think I'm in love with the way they said it was good. I'm scared. If I do something bad, please don't let it be them.' The ink at 'them' has run, as if a drop had fallen on it, a salt-dry circle with a faint grey rim.

n5.text: You put the plank back exactly as it was. You straighten the chair. You set the warm roll on the table with a note you don't remember writing: 'from the baker, for you.' As you step out through the front door, a twig snaps in the trees behind the Nook, and a pale scarf-end slips behind a trunk a second too late. 'Don't tell anyone,' a voice says, from nowhere, small and shaky and almost normal. 'Please.' You don't turn around. 'I won't,' you say, to the forest. A long breath answers you, and then footsteps going away, very quickly, running.

n1.text: It started as a vibration in the soles of your feet, the third night. By the fifth you could feel it in your teeth. Now, standing in the upstairs hall at dusk, you can hear it plainly: a low hum, like a hive or a refrigerator or a very large animal purring in its sleep. It comes from the wall at the end of the hall, the patched square at knee height next to the ritual room door, and the wallpaper circles around it seem to be arranged in a spiral. The hum has a pitch. If you hold your breath, you can almost tell which note.

wahl.label: Press your ear to the wall
Put your palm flat on the patch

n2.text: Cold plaster against your cheek. The hum comes apart into layers: a drone, a rhythmic tapping, and a thin, thin sound on top of both, like wind through a keyhole, which slowly becomes a voice. A woman's voice, murmuring, a lullaby in German you half understand. 'Schlaf, mein Kind, schlaf ein...' Then, clearer: 'Shh. Shh. Not yet. They'll hear you.' The voice breaks off in a little gasp, and for a moment there's absolute silence, and then something presses back against your ear from the other side, soft and round and very slightly warm, like a forehead.

n3.text: You find the note, a low, shaky B-flat, and send it out into the hall. The hum falters. It stops for a half-second, and you have time to think: how stupid. Then it comes back, matching you, slightly lower, the way a child copies a lullaby: close, but not quite. You hum a higher note. It follows. The wallpaper circles seem to turn, very slowly, and the whole upstairs hall fills up with a faint sweet sound like a hundred voices softly singing along. You stop in the middle of a breath. The hall carries on, perfectly in tune, for four more bars, and then stops where you stopped, as if it had been waiting for your cue.

wahl.label: Press your ear to the wall

n4.text: The plaster is warm, damp, faintly springy, and under your hand the patch pulses once, twice, like a pulse in a wrist. A hairline crack opens from under your palm and runs up the wall, silent, quick, all the way to the ceiling, and from the crack a very faint puff of dust drifts out that smells, you realise with horror, of baby powder. The hum stops dead. In the sudden silence you hear a tiny wet click from inside the wall, the sound a very small mouth makes when it opens.

wahl.label: Take your hand away at once

n5.text: 'Lizzy?' Your own voice sounds absurd, but the house heard it. The tapping starts again, slow, tap, tap, tap, and the faint voice behind the plaster says, tired, amused, quite close: 'Not Lizzy. Lizzy has gone. She left a very long time ago.' A pause. 'But she said somebody would come. She said somebody would listen.' Another pause, very small. 'Are you the one who can read?' Before you can answer, something in the wall sighs, relieved, and the hum slides down a whole tone, content, like a cat settling on a lap, and does not come back that night.

n1.text: In the bakery the round woman is wrapping one single day-old roll, so slowly that you realise she's stalling. 'It's the ninth,' she says, to the roll. 'He'll come in at four like every year and buy a loaf and say it's for the foxes. Nobody has ever told him I know.' She presses her mouth together. 'I bake him one every year and I never have the courage to give it.' She looks at you, hopeful and ashamed. 'You could. If you wanted. But it would cost you the afternoon, mind.'

wahl.label: Take the roll to the Nook
wahl.folge: You walk out into the fog

n2.text: He opens the door with flour on his cheek and sees the roll and doesn't understand it. 'It's the day-old stuff, I don't need...' He looks at your face, at the paper, at the small pencil candle drawn on it, and something happens in his throat. 'Who told you?' Nobody did, you say, somebody only knew. He turns his back on you and stands facing the wall. 'Nobody knows,' he says to the planks. 'I don't know. It's a guess, I counted the winters.' His shoulders go up and down, very slightly. 'Don't look. I'm NOT... I'm just cold.'

wahl.label: Look at the wall with him

n3.text: 'Honey. Cinnamon. Things that go on a fire,' says the baker, counting on floury fingers. 'And he stares at the rye with the seeds like it's the moon. He's never bought one. It costs more.' She names the price, and it is the last of the coins in your pocket. On the shelf the rye sits heavy and dark and scattered with seeds. She doesn't push. She wipes the counter very thoroughly with her back half turned, and waits for you to decide how much an afternoon is worth.

wahl.label: Spend your last coins on the rye
wahl.folge: You walk to the Nook with the rye, and nothing in your pocket

wahl.label: Take the plain roll only
wahl.folge: You walk out into the fog

n4.text: You look at the wall with him. It's a good wall, roughly planed, with a nail where the coat goes and a knothole shaped like a mouth. After a while his breathing steadies, the sleeve goes over his face once, quick, and he turns around with red eyes and his chin up. 'It's a roll,' he says, aggressively. 'It's a good roll.' He holds it with both hands, the way you hold something that could be taken back. 'Sit. I'm not eating it alone, that would be sad.' He tears it in half, and the sound is the loudest thing that has happened in the Nook all year.

wahl.label: Sit down and eat with him
wahl.folge: He lights the stove for you

wahl.label: Ask how old he thinks he is

n5.text: 'Don't,' he says into the wall, and then, as if he tripped over it, 'say it again. NOT that I... just. Once more.' You say it. He nods hard, twice, like a man agreeing to a verdict. When he turns around his face is blotchy and furious and wet, and he wipes it on the scarf without shame. 'I made a wish,' he says. 'Don't ask. If I tell, it doesn't...' He bites the roll in two, gives you the larger half and sits on the floor with his back against the stove, and the Nook feels, for a minute, the size of one person's happiness.

wahl.label: Sit on the floor with him

n6.text: He sees the rye before he sees you, and his face does something complicated and furious. 'That costs more,' he says. 'That's the seeded one. Take it back, I can't... how much was it, I've got a jar, I'll...' He's already dragging a jam jar from under the bench and shaking out coppers, until you tell him it's a present and he stops with the jar in both hands. 'You paid for this,' he says, slowly, 'because of a day I don't even know is real.' He puts the jar down. He puts the rye on the table and looks at it the way you look at a lit window from the road. 'I'm not cutting it today,' he says. 'It's too good to start.'

wahl.label: Cut it for him
wahl.folge: He holds the first slice with both hands

wahl.label: Leave it whole on the table
wahl.folge: He keeps glancing at it all evening

n1.text: The drawing book lies open on the table when you come in, a child's one with a cardboard cover and a horse on it, and Noah is outside somewhere, only the kettle breathing on the stove. The page is crayon, pressed hard: a table with two cups on it. A blue one with a fox. A plain brown one, with a tiny wobbly smile of steam. Between them, in careful letters: THE TWO CUPS. And beneath, almost not there: what if it's every day. The back door bangs, he's inside, snow on his shoulders, and he sees you, and he sees the book.

wahl.label: Tell him you like it, and tell him something true about you

n2.text: 'It's bad,' says Noah. 'The perspective's wrong, the cups are too big...' He stops. He has heard what you told him, a small true thing, and weighs it, and sets one down beside it. 'I draw things I want to be true. That's the rule. If I draw them enough it's like practising.' He comes and stands next to you, stiff, almost touching, and turns a page, and another: a fox with five tails, a hut with a chimney. Then a page that is black from edge to edge, scratched through until the paper tore. He doesn't stop on it. 'This one,' he says, brighter, 'this one's you.'

wahl.label: Look at the drawing of you

n3.text: You close it very gently, thumb on the horse. He watches the cover instead of you. 'You can look,' he says. 'It's only drawing.' You both know it isn't. 'I'm not good at people,' he says, to the book. 'Faces go wrong. But I did one. If you wanted. It's the only one I did in colour.' He sits on the crate opposite with the book against his chest, hugging it, ears red. The sentence hangs there, tiny and brave, waiting to see whether it will be stepped on.

n4.text: It is you. Obviously, because of the crooked collar and the slouch, but the face has been made with an unreasonable amount of love, every freckle, yellow for the lamp, green for the forest behind you. He has put you at the table with the brown cup, and the colour of the cup is exactly the colour of the one in your hands now. At the bottom, a date from last week and four words: the one who stayed. 'It's bad,' says Noah. 'Don't say it's good. If it's good I'll have to...' He swallows. 'I'll have to keep drawing.'

wahl.label: Ask if you can keep it
Tell him to keep drawing
wahl.folge: He bites his lip and nods

n5.text: 'It's okay. I'm not that kind of...' He turns the book over and over. 'Fine. If you promise not to laugh.' He finds the page and slides it across the table with one finger, as if it might go off. It's you, the crooked collar, the brown cup, the lamp-light in yellow, and at the bottom: the one who stayed. You laugh, not at it, a breath of a laugh that breaks halfway, and he looks up sharply, terrified, and then understands, and half smiles back.

wahl.label: Ask if you can keep it
Tell him to keep drawing
wahl.folge: He bites his lip and nods

n6.text: Noah takes the page in both hands and can't tear it. He has to try three times. It's the quiet kind of tearing, slow, along the spine, as if the paper hurt. When it comes free he looks at it a long second, the way you look at a thing for the last time, and gives it to you. 'It's not for sad days,' he says. 'It's for when you're far away and you can't remember if I was real.' He goes red to the scarf. 'I mean it's for a wall. Put it on a wall.' In the book, the page that's left has only a table and one cup.

wahl.label: Put it away carefully
wahl.folge: You carry his drawing with you

n7.text: 'Yeah,' says Noah. 'Kids'.' He shuts the horse over the crayon with a very small click and slides the book under the bench, and says brightly that it's going to snow, that the kettle's nearly on, that he's got cookies. 'They're burnt on one side,' he says. 'Sorry.' All of it a little too fast, and nothing he says has a single true thing in it. The book stays under the bench. You can see the corner of it. For a long time he doesn't look at that corner, so carefully that it is all he looks at.

wahl.label: Say nothing and drink your tea
wahl.folge: The corner of the book stays there

ort.gymnasium.k4.text: Without kids the school feels like a held breath. It's Sunday and every door is locked, but the lights in the long corridor are on, a line of cold white lamps buzzing quietly. At the far end one door is open and a man's shadow lies across the floor. In the classroom the globe has been turned so that your little town faces the window, and next to it, in red pencil, someone drew a slightly crooked circle with three dots inside, a line from the circle to the castle, and from the castle a thin line straight down. Below the floor.

optionen.name: Look at the red pencil lines
optionen.text: Under the lines there's a short sentence in neat board handwriting: THE ONE WHO WAS GIVEN IS THE DOOR. And below it, smaller: ASK NOAH ABOUT THE SOUND.

optionen.name: Check Connor's desk drawer
optionen.text: Locked. But the keyhole is wide, and when you shine your phone into it you see a stack of photos, all of the same child at different ages, each one a bit more frightened, each one a bit stiller.

varianten.beitritt: The school is open for you on a Sunday. Connor's key turns in the lock for you, a little iron click, and nobody stops you in the corridor. The red pencil lines on the globe are fresh, and the circle next to your house has a second circle drawn around it, in a different handwriting, softer, with a tiny smile inside it.

ort.haus.k4.text: You've stopped noticing the smell, and THAT is the scary part. The house has settled around you like a coat. The floor stripe, the warm cup, the faint hum behind the patched wall, it all feels normal now, like furniture. The warm door stands open all day and you can walk past it without flinching. Today you notice that the circles in the wallpaper are arranged in groups of three, and that the stain on the floor of the warm room has moved a little toward the patched wall. Something has been dragged, slowly, over many days. Toward you.

optionen.name: Examine the patch on the wall
optionen.text: Up close the plaster is covered in hair-thin cracks that radiate from one spot at knee height, as if something pushed from the inside. You press your ear to it. Very quietly, and very far away, someone is humming a lullaby.

optionen.name: Go to bed
optionen.text: You sleep, and for the first time you dream of nothing. In the morning there's a full warm cup next to the bed, and a small clean footprint in the dust on the outside windowsill, on the second floor.

varianten.beitritt: The hum in the walls has your tune in it now, the one from the church. You catch yourself humming along as you take your coat off, and you stop, and the humming goes on a beat without you. The warm door is wide open, and for the first time the room beyond it looks like it was set for guests.

ort.lunuen.k4.text: The town has stopped pretending, and you can tell. On a Sunday morning every shop is shut, every curtain drawn, and the few people in the street walk fast with their heads down, like it's the middle of a storm. Every window has a candle in it, and every candle burns at the same height. The church bell rings once, and a few seconds later it rings once again, off by a small awful fraction of a beat, like a skipped heart. In front of the bakery someone chalked the circle with three dots on the pavement, and people step carefully around it.

optionen.name: Step on the chalk circle
optionen.text: Nothing happens. But three doors across the street open at once, and three people stand in the doorways and look at you without any expression. You step off, and one by one they close their doors.

optionen.name: Ask the baker through the closed door why the town is shut
optionen.text: 'Because we have an important day coming, dear,' she says softly. 'And you wouldn't want to be out in the street.' Then, even softer: 'Please be in your house on the night of the new moon.'

varianten.beitritt: The people on the street nod at you now, small deep nods, as if you were part of their family. A woman you've never met presses your hand and says, 'Welcome,' and an old man with a candle falls into step beside you, a half-pace behind, like an honour guard. Nobody asks where you're going. Everybody seems to know.

ort.nook.k4.text: The Nook is dark when you arrive and quiet in a way that feels wrong for a house that's usually ticking and humming. The shutters are closed, the stove is cold, and there's only a single candle burning low next to an open book of children's drawings. Someone has drawn the same picture again and again: a small figure with a scarf standing between two bigger figures, one with a kind face and one with no face at all. Noah sits in the corner with his knees pulled up, rocking a little, a tiny radio playing cheerful music so low it's only a murmur.

optionen.name: Sit next to him quietly
optionen.text: He doesn't look at you for a long time. When he does, his eyes are red but dry and his smile is perfect. 'Oh, it's you. You scared me. I was just resting. It's fine. I'm fine. Don't look at the drawings, they're old.'

optionen.name: Turn the pages of the drawing book
optionen.text: The last page has a tall figure in a doorway, drawn in thick black crayon, and under it, in a different, adult hand: THIS IS NOT YOU. DON'T LET IT OUT.

varianten.begegnung: Noah has been waiting in the dark for you. The radio is off this time. 'I knew it was you,' he says to the wall, not turning. 'I heard the way you walk. You walk like someone who's got a key in their pocket.' His voice is flat and gentle. 'Sit, idiot. Don't say anything. I just want someone to be in the room.'

ort.see.k4.text: Sunday morning at the lake, cold and clear, the sky hard and blue, and the fog lying only on the water like a lid. Forty people in dark coats stand along the shore, shoulder to shoulder, facing the lake in complete silence. Nobody prays, nobody sings, they just watch it the way you'd watch a sleeping animal you are fond of. Every now and then the surface rings in the middle, a slow wide circle that spreads and dies at the shore. Over the water, in the white, a faint shape seems to lean in and look back at the town.

optionen.name: Look at the fog above the water
optionen.text: It moves against the wind. When it drifts over the crowd, each person takes a small breath in, one after another, and lets it out a second later in perfect time.

optionen.name: Look at Connor at the front of the crowd
optionen.text: He stands a little apart and closer to the water than the others, hands folded behind his back. Around his neck hangs a thin chain with a small iron key, and where the fog touches it, it glows faintly orange. It's the key to the castle, you realise, and he wears it like a priest wears a cross.

optionen.name: Read the notice board at the playground
optionen.text: Between the lost-cat flyers there's a hand-drawn map of the castle grounds with an X on the east side, and under it, in the same round handwriting as the Nook note: ASK ME ABOUT THE BASEMENT. NOT HIM. ME.

varianten.beitritt: The crowd makes a gap for you, and you step into it, and it closes behind you with a soft sound of coats. Forty people, shoulder to shoulder, and you are one of them, facing the water. The fog above the lake leans in, and for a moment it feels as if the lake is greeting you by name.

ort.wald.k4.text: The forest is cold and bright today, every branch edged with frost, and it looks smaller somehow, the path to the hill shorter, the scorched patch smaller, as if the whole place has been shrinking away from you since you stopped being afraid. The circles on the trunks are fresh, sharp-edged, pale wood showing in the cuts. Not Noah's work, these were made with a real blade and a steady hand. On the highest scorched rock sits a neat little offering: three candles, a loaf of bread, and a child's mitten.

optionen.name: Look at the mitten
optionen.text: Small, red, hand-knitted, scorched along one edge. Someone stitched a tiny N into the cuff with black thread and then pulled the thread out again, leaving only the holes.

optionen.name: Blow out one of the candles
optionen.text: It relights itself the moment you turn away. You only notice when your own shadow jumps on the tree in front of you.

varianten.wiederbesuch: The offering on the rock is fresh again: new candles, new bread, and the mitten in the same position as before, but turned so the stitched N faces the town. Someone has been here since you left, and you start to understand that someone does this every day.

n1.text: The crowd breaks up and drifts away from the shore, one by one, until it's just the two of you, the grey water, and your own breath. Connor turns to face you. The mask is still there, but thinner now, like old paper. 'Thank you for coming, friend. I know you've guessed. You're clever, so I'll say it plainly. I lead them. I have for a very long time.' He lays a hand on his chest. 'We are not monsters. We are keepers. We keep something that would otherwise harm this valley. Your great-grandmother kept it with us until the end.' He holds out his hand, palm up. 'Join us. Be kept, and keep. It's very peaceful. You'll never be lonely again.'

wahl.label: Ask what exactly you'd be keeping
wahl.folge: Connor explains his side of the story

n2.text: His hand is warm and dry, and the moment you touch it a sound goes through you like a bell, from the soles of your feet to your skull. The water gives one enormous ripple, and every person on the far shore, hundreds of meters away, turns their head to look at you. Connor closes his other hand over yours. 'Welcome,' he says, and he means it, and that's the worst part. 'There are things I can tell you now. About the boy. About what sleeps under the castle. About the room in your house. Walk with me.'

wahl.label: Walk with him
wahl.folge: Connor tells the player about Noah and the cellar

wahl.label: Pull your hand away, too late

n3.text: 'Something very old and very tired.' He looks past you at the water. 'When a person dies the wrong way, they don't always stay dead. Our old leader, Dorothy, the dearest woman, left us in the cruelest way. We tried to bring her back. We were so sure she wanted to come.' His eyes are wet. 'It went wrong. And what came instead has to be kept quiet, and warm, and fed. We're not the ones who did the harm, friend. We're the ones who clean up after it.' He is so sincere that it's very hard not to believe him.

n4.text: He doesn't argue. He lowers his hand and smiles a little, an old man's tired kind smile. 'Most people don't say yes the first time.' He steps back, hands behind his back. 'But remember, friend, the door is always open. And be careful of the boy. It's gentle of you to like him. But he is not as gentle as he looks. Neither is the thing behind his eyes.' He turns and walks away into the fog without looking back.

wahl.label: Watch him go
wahl.folge: The player did not join; Connor's insider help is lost

n5.text: He leads you up the shore path, away from the others, and tells it low and soft like a bedtime story. 'The boy's name is Noah. He was ours before he was anyone's. When he was small we tried something sacred on him, up on the hill. It went... partially well.' The word 'partially' lands like a stone. 'There is a place under the castle where the old magic sleeps. A hidden door in the east wing, behind a shelf, and this key will open the last lock.' He lays a small iron key in your hand. 'Go and look. Do NOT take what you find. And do not let it near him. Promise me this one thing.'

wahl.label: Promise
wahl.folge: The player carries the key and the cult's trust

wahl.label: Ask what happens if Noah gets near it

n6.text: 'Too late, friend,' he says kindly, 'but that's alright. Everyone tries that.' The ripple in the water has died and the far shore is empty again. He doesn't force you. He doesn't need to. 'Come with me. I'll tell you what I promised.' And he does, in a low steady voice, all the way up the shore path, while the fog follows you both like a pet.

wahl.label: Follow him
wahl.folge: The player is a member in all but willingness

n7.text: His smile does not move. 'Memory, mostly,' he says. 'Attention. Names. A little warmth. A town can feed something old for a long, long time, if it does so with love.' He says it exactly like a gardener talking about compost. 'Nothing in the world is hurt by it. You'll see. Come to the supper. Meet the others.' He tilts his head. 'And keep an eye on the boy for us, would you? He sleeps badly.'

n8.text: 'He touched it once, as a child.' Connor's voice is flat, and for the first time he does not smile. 'He woke up in his bed and everyone told him it was a dream. It was kinder. But what slept in him has been waking ever since, a little each year. If the cube stands near him, it wakes all the way.' He closes your fingers around the key. 'Promise me you will not bring them together. Promise me.'

wahl.label: Promise
wahl.folge: The player carries the key and the cult's trust

wahl.label: Say nothing
wahl.folge: Connor reads the silence as consent

varianten.beitritt: Connor stops you on the shore, mid-step. 'You've already said yes, friend. Not with words, but you've said it. The supper, the church, the key at your throat.' He lays a hand on his chest. 'I only need you to say it out loud, once, so the water can hear you.' Behind him, forty people turn their faces to the lake, in silence, waiting.

n1.text: You find him on the bench as the day dies, as if he'd never left. 'Hey,' says Mika, and tilts his head back to blow smoke at the sky. 'So. You met him on the shore, huh? The big talk. The hand. I felt that from here, man.' He stretches his arm along the backrest, relaxed. Then he turns his head and really looks at you, and the lazy eyes sharpen like a camera finding focus. 'Be honest with me. Did you take it?'

wahl.label: Tell him it's none of his business

n2.text: The smoke stops coming out of his mouth. For a second it looks like someone cut a wire in him. 'Ah.' It's a very small sound. 'Okay.' He drops the cigarette and grinds it out with his heel, slowly, thoroughly, like he's killing something. When he looks up he's still smiling, and for the first time it's real, thin and cold as a razor. 'I won't lie to you, man. I hate them. Every last one, in their dark coats with their candles and sweet faces. They're so boring. And they're so SURE.' He stands, and for a second he seems taller. 'So I'm going to try and talk you out of it. Directly. Like a friend. Take the hand back. Leave this valley.'

n3.text: 'Ha!' He claps once, delighted, a soft sound like a stone in water. 'I KNEW it. You've got a good head, man.' He leans back, glowing. 'Okay, here's a gift, completely free: there's a door under the castle. You've been told not to go in. Fine. Don't. Or do. I think you should. It's the only fun thing left in this town, honestly.' His eyes slide left, then right. 'East wing. Look behind the books. Take whatever you want. Or don't. That's the best part. Everything's optional.'

wahl.label: Say thanks
wahl.folge: Mika claps you on the shoulder

n4.text: 'Fair.' He raises both hands. 'Totally fair, man.' He's still smiling, but his eyes are somewhere over your shoulder. He lights a new cigarette from the glowing tip of the old one, though the old one isn't there anymore. 'Anyway. The sky's gonna turn soon. Go home. Don't go left around the lake tonight, the left way is closed.' He tips an imaginary hat. 'Or go left. What do I know. I just sit here.'

n5.text: 'Me? I'm a fan of good stories, man.' He looks at the water for a very long time. 'And the story with you in it hasn't ended yet. Plus.' He rubs his jaw. 'They keep feeding me their dead and calling it a prayer. It gets old. I'd like a different kind of ending, just once.' He laughs, short and bright, and the whole lake behind him laughs along, one dull echo from the far shore. 'Anyway! Go home. Sleep. Or don't. Bye.'

wahl.label: Walk away
wahl.folge: Mika's hint level goes up to 2

n6.text: 'Yeah,' he says quietly. 'Yeah. It always is.' He rubs his face with both hands. When he lets go, he looks very old for a second, then boyish again. 'Okay. Go see the castle then. East wing, behind the books. Whatever you find, don't give it to him. Don't give it to ANYONE.' He studies you. 'And if you see the kid at the bottom of the stairs, be nice. Just be nice.' He lights a fresh cigarette. 'It won't help. But be nice anyway.'

wahl.label: Leave him on the bench
wahl.folge: Mika's hint level goes up to 3

varianten.beitritt: Mika doesn't wave. His cigarette is already out, and he is sitting very straight on the bench. 'I smelled it on you from across the lake,' he says. 'Clove and cold iron and Connor's good soap.' He doesn't smile. 'I'm going to ask you one more time, and I want you to think about it. Do you want to be one of them?'
varianten.mika_hint: He looks at you for a long moment, and then laughs, short and soft. 'You're starting to see it. Aren't you.' He taps ash into the fog. 'That's good, man. That's really good. That's more than most of them ever get.' Behind him, the lake rings once, a slow wide circle, and for a second you can't tell who laughed first.

n1.text: You say Connor's name. Just once, casually, as you step into the Nook. The kettle that was singing stops in the middle of a note. Noah, halfway through a sentence about cinnamon, goes completely still, the cup stopped on its way to his mouth, a muscle in his jaw jumping like something under his skin has turned over in its sleep. 'Where did you hear that name?' he says, very evenly. Then, much faster, in his high bright voice: 'Never mind! Everyone knows Connor! He's so nice! He brings soup! Do you want a cookie?' His hands shake so hard the cup rattles in the saucer.

wahl.label: Put a hand on his shoulder
Tell him you saw Connor at the lake

n2.text: He flinches so hard he nearly drops the cup, and then, slowly, the shaking eases and he leans into your hand like a cat, eyes shut. 'I'm okay,' he whispers. 'I'm always okay.' He's smiling, and tears run down his cheeks without a sound, and he doesn't seem to notice. 'It's not like I want you to stay. It's just, if you could stay a bit... that would be fine.' The stove ticks. 'Just don't let him take you somewhere alone. Please.'

wahl.label: Promise you won't go anywhere alone with him

n3.text: 'What did he say?' The cheerful voice is gone. This one is flat and fast. 'Did he give you anything? A key? Did he touch you? Did he tell you where?' He grabs your sleeve with both hands, knuckles white. Then he catches himself, lets go and laughs, awkward, bright, awful. 'Sorry! That was weird. I'm being weird.' He stares at the floor. 'If he gave you a key, don't use it. Please. I'm asking as a friend. I don't have many.'

wahl.label: Promise you won't use it
wahl.folge: Noah's trust goes up, though you may break it

wahl.label: Say you have to see for yourself

n4.text: 'Oh. Okay. Thanks.' He's so relieved it's almost painful. He talks about cookies and the roof and a squirrel in the kitchen while his hands slowly stop shaking, and by the end of the hour he's laughing for real, head back, scarf slipping. In the lamplight he looks so young that something in your chest hurts. He says nothing more about Connor. But when you leave he stays at the door until you're out of sight, and he never once blinks.

wahl.label: Walk home
wahl.folge: Noah is a bit more attached

n5.text: 'Right.' It's not his voice. 'Of course.' His hands fold in his lap, neat and still, and he looks at you, calm and polite, and for the first time you see how old his eyes are. 'You do what you have to do.' A pause. The smile stretches, just a bit. 'We'll see each other soon, I'm sure.' It's not a threat. It's worse. It's a plan. A second later he blinks and he's the bright little guy again, scratching his neck. 'What? Why are you looking at me like that? Idiot.'

wahl.label: Leave quietly
wahl.folge: A seed of the other Noah is planted

varianten.begegnung: You haven't even said anything, and Noah is already standing in the doorway, pale, with the kettle in one hand like a weapon. 'Don't,' he says. 'Whatever it is. Don't bring his name in here.' A long pause. 'Okay. You can. I'll make tea. Just don't say it twice.'

n1.text: The path up the hill is steeper than it looked, and the farther you climb the less grows beside it, until the last stretch is bare grey stone and black soil. At the top the whole valley lies below you like a map laid out for a child: the town with its candles, the lake like a coin, the castle small and dark on its rise. Right in front of you the earth is scorched in a perfect circle, forty feet across, and in the middle of it stands a small wooden chair, charred black on one side and worn smooth on the other, facing the town. Someone has left a pair of white flowers on the seat.

wahl.label: Look at the town from here

n2.text: It's warm. Not from the sun. The seat is warm in the shape of a small person, and when you lean back, the charred slats hold you in a grip so gentle that it takes you a moment to understand you can't get up. Your hands lie on the armrests. Under your fingers, you find carvings: a child's name, N, scratched with a nail, and under it, over and over, a dozen small crude tallies. The wind brings smoke, though there is nothing burning, and with it a smell you will never forget: hair, wool, sweet and rotten, and under it, thin and high and impossibly far away, someone screaming for his mother. It stops. The chair lets go of you.

wahl.label: Look at the town from here

n3.text: You circle the edge of the scorch, careful not to step inside, and notice that the ground is not uniformly black. Along one side, small and neat, six holes have been dug in a row at exact intervals, and in each hole stands a candle stub planted upright in ash. Six. And the seventh hole, at the end, is empty, but fresh. The dirt around it is dark and damp, as though somebody had dug it only this morning. It's about the size of a small coffin, or a shoebox.

wahl.label: Look at the town from here

n4.text: From the chair's angle, every lit window in Lünen points up at you. You can see the church, small and yellow, and next to it the bakery, and the school with its row of dark classrooms, and the long dark road to the lake. You can see the Nook's chimney smoke curling into the evening, tiny and thin. And you realise why the chair faces the town. Whoever sat here was meant to see all of them, every single one, looking up. Looking at him. Down in the valley, very small, one light is moving up the hill road, a lantern or a phone, steady, patient, coming this way.

wahl.label: Stay and wait for whoever it is

n5.text: You take the downhill path fast, and the air gets warmer and the sounds come back with every step, birds, your own boots, the stream. At the bottom of the slope, where the first normal oaks begin, you glance back once. From down here the chair is only a speck on the ridge. But it has been turned. When you left it faced the valley. Now it faces you.

n6.text: You wait. The light climbs. In twenty minutes it becomes a man in a dark coat, a lantern in one hand and a thermos in the other, climbing the last meters with the ease of someone who has done it a thousand times. He stops at the edge of the burnt circle and doesn't come in. 'Ah,' says Connor, quietly, without surprise. 'You found the hill.' He sets the lantern on a rock. 'I come up every Sunday. To keep him company, you understand. It seems only right.' He pours something hot into the thermos lid and holds it out across the line of the circle, and you realise he's offering it not to you but to the empty chair.

n7.text: He sets the cup on the seat, very gently, next to the white flowers, and bows his head for exactly as long as a prayer. 'Nobody should be alone in the dark,' he says, to the chair. 'Not even for one night.' Then he turns his calm, tired eyes on you and smiles. 'You came on your own, friend. That is a good sign. Most people have to be led here.' He picks up the lantern. 'Come to the lake on Sunday morning. I'll tell you all about it.' He walks away down the path, and the cup of tea on the chair goes on steaming into the dark, long after he has gone.

n8.text: 'A very small boy.' Connor looks at the chair for a long moment. 'We did it for love, you understand. We were so sure. She was the dearest woman in the valley, and she had gone, and we couldn't bear the quiet.' His face doesn't change. 'He was very brave. The bravest child I have ever known. He didn't scream, you know, not once, until the end.' He lowers his lantern. 'Which is why we could never leave him alone afterwards. It would have been the cruellest thing.' There's no joke in his voice, no cruelty, only a tender sadness, and that's the part that makes the wind on the hill feel suddenly very cold.

n1.text: The warm door has been open for days. Tonight you go in. The room is smaller than you thought, bare floorboards, no furniture, one round window painted over from the inside in a dark brown that might once have been white. The circle on the floor is scratched so deep that the splinters are pale. Burnt candle stubs stand at its edge, thirteen of them, evenly spaced, and in the very middle there's a dark stain the size of a small body. The patched square in the wall stands to your left, newer than the plaster around it, and the whole room smells of milk and candle wax and something sweeter underneath.

wahl.label: Kneel and look at the stain
Scratch at the edge of the patch

n2.text: Your boots find the grooves in the floor, and your whole body goes quiet, as if someone had put a hand over the volume of the world. The circle isn't big. It's exactly the right size for one person lying down with their arms at their sides. You are standing on the spot where a person's chest would be. Under your feet, the boards are warm, and warmer, and a faint tap comes up through the soles, and another, a very slow heartbeat. Every candle stub around you flickers, though none of them is lit. 'Welcome back,' says a voice in the wall, tender and amused, 'welcome back, Elisabeth,' and your name, your real name, comes in right after it, in the same soft singsong, like a lullaby you used to know.

wahl.label: Step out of the circle fast

n3.text: You kneel at the edge of the dark patch. Up close it isn't a stain, it's a shape, a thin layer of something dried into the wood: the outline of a child's body, curled up on its side, knees to chest, like a sleeper. Around it, in the grain, a faint white residue like salt. Like old milk. You touch it with a fingertip. It's tacky. At the head of the shape, right where the face would be, there's a tiny brown handprint, a finger-width wide, pressed into the wood as if by someone who had been trying very hard not to be left.

wahl.label: Scratch at the edge of the patch

n4.text: The plaster at the edge of the patch flakes off under your nail, grey and chalky and cold. Behind it is something soft. A layer of rough cloth, brownish, rotten, with a thin crust of lime, and under the cloth, hard against your fingertip, something smooth and round and curved, the size of a walnut, like the top of a very small skull. You pull your hand back as if it had bitten you. From inside the wall, a very quiet tapping starts, a knuckle, a fingernail, a baby's rattle, no longer rhythmic. Eager.

n5.text: You retreat to the doorway and your heels catch on the threshold, and you stumble backwards into the hall, and the door swings shut in front of you with a soft, final click. You stand in the hallway with the clean stripe at your feet and the hum in your teeth. Behind the door, in the room you just left, a single candle has lit itself in the circle. You can see it through the keyhole: small, white, exactly in the middle. Waiting.

n6.text: 'I'm not Lizzy,' you say, and your voice sounds small. The room goes quiet. All the candles are very still. 'No,' says the voice in the wall, after a long, long pause. 'No. You're not.' It sounds so disappointed that your throat closes. 'You're her blood, though. You're very like her. Tell me, child, did she send you? Did she send you to read?' Something in the plaster shifts, a soft damp turning over. 'I have been so patient,' it whispers. You are suddenly aware that you're standing in the exact center of the circle and have been for some time.

wahl.label: Step out of the circle fast

n1.text: He has been hiding something behind his back since you came in, and it makes him walk like a crab, sideways, chin high, ears red. 'Sit. Not there. THERE. Close your eyes. It's NOT that I made it for you, idiot, I had wood left over.' You close them. Something is put into your hands, small, light, warm from his pockets, carved. When you look it's a cup, a little wooden cup with a fox cut into the side and, under it, in clumsy letters like a child's, your name. The rim is sanded as soft as skin. 'It's so there's a second one,' he says. 'In case the first is... in case I'm not here.'

wahl.label: Tell him it's the best gift you've ever been given

n2.text: 'It's not even straight,' he says. It is, though, and you can see how many evenings are in it, the nicks where he started again, the shavings he kept to light the stove. He rubs his thumb over the fox as if he couldn't leave it alone. 'You don't have to,' he says, with enormous casualness. 'But you could take it. With you. When you go. So it's not here with all the... it's somewhere that's...' He gives up on the sentence. 'Somewhere else. Where nothing can happen to it.'

wahl.label: Say you'll carry it everywhere
wahl.folge: He smiles and then hides it

wahl.label: Say you'll leave it here, for next time

n3.text: 'I didn't say that.' It trips on its way out. 'People go. You go home, or the house...' He stops, and the stove ticks, and he finds the next words slowly. 'Sometimes I don't know where I've been. You know that. I'd rather there was a thing that stayed.' He pushes his hair back and you see a small mark at the temple, blue-yellow at the edges, and he sees you see it and says, mildly, 'I walked into the door.' It's the voice of someone who has said that sentence to people who wanted it to be true.

wahl.label: Take the door as a good enough reason
wahl.folge: He's grateful, and ashamed of being grateful

wahl.label: Take his hand and say you believe in the cup
wahl.folge: He smiles and then hides it

n4.text: It fits into your coat pocket as if it had been measured for it, which, you suddenly realise, it was. He pours tea into the wooden cup and the blue one and lets you hold both. 'You can put things in it. A coin. A stone. Whatever you don't want to lose.' He's looking at the stove again. 'There's one thing,' he says. 'Don't look at the door while I ask. Promise you'll drink from it, on a day I'm not there. Just once. It'll be a bit like I was. Not so you'd notice.'

wahl.label: Promise, without looking at the door
wahl.folge: He lets out all his air

wahl.label: Hold the wooden cup and just nod
wahl.folge: He takes it as a yes

n5.text: 'For next time,' he says, and turns the words over. 'Yeah. Okay.' He puts the little cup on the shelf beside the blue one, and the shelf looks different, as if it had been waiting. 'I'll wash it every morning,' says Noah, like somebody promising to learn a language. 'So it's ready. NOT because I... idiot, don't look at me like that.' At the door he holds it open and doesn't say goodbye, because he doesn't know it's a word that can be used for somebody coming back.

wahl.label: Say 'see you tomorrow'
wahl.folge: He holds the door a second longer than necessary

wahl.label: Leave without a word
wahl.folge: He watches you go into the fog

n6.text: You keep your eyes on the knothole, the one shaped like a mouth, and say it, and mean it. 'Okay,' says Noah, and his voice is very small. 'Okay. You didn't look.' He takes a breath that goes all the way down. 'That's the first one I ever asked for, you know. A promise. It was a lot smaller in my head.' He laughs at himself, wetly, and pushes the wooden cup an inch deeper into your palm. 'It's yours now. Don't give it back, that's the rule.'

wahl.label: Put it in your pocket
wahl.folge: It sits warm against your leg

wahl.label: Drink from it right now
wahl.folge: It tastes of honey, and wood, and him

n7.text: He decides to take the nod as a yes, and you can see him deciding it, the way you watch somebody put a heavy bag down on purpose. 'Good,' he says. 'Good. It doesn't need words, that's... that's better.' He stirs his own tea much longer than necessary. 'If I'm not here and it's cold and the road is long,' he says, 'it's the cup from the Nook. That's what it is. That's all it is.' It is, he doesn't say, all he's got to send.

wahl.label: Put it in your pocket
wahl.folge: It sits warm against your leg

n1.text: The record player is older than both of you together, a hand-cranked box with a horn the colour of tea, and he has to turn the handle thirty times before it plays. The record has no sleeve, only a handwritten label, Debussy, Clair de Lune, grey with handling. Noah sits on the floor in front of it with his knees up, and when the first notes come, soft and wrong-speed and crackling, his whole face unfolds. All the sarcasm drains out of it, all the bracing. 'This is the one thing I'm not scared of,' he says. 'Don't talk. Please. Not until it's over.'

n2.text: It lasts five minutes and it's the longest you've ever listened to anything. The notes come out of the horn like water over stone, the stove ticks along, and Noah rocks a quarter inch forward and back with his eyes shut. Halfway through, he reaches without looking and finds the hem of your sleeve and holds it between two fingers, so lightly that you could break it by breathing. You don't. When the needle hisses in the groove, neither of you moves. 'Again,' he says. 'Once more. And then I'll let you go home. Promise.'

wahl.label: Say you must go before dark

n3.text: You watch him instead. You shouldn't, probably, but there is nobody in the room you could give it back to. His lips move along with the melody without a sound, he knows every fall of it, he has learned it the way a child learns a prayer. The stove-light moves on the scarf, and when the record crackles on a scratch he winces as if it were his own. At the end he opens his eyes and sees you looking. After a while he says, 'You looked at me.' He doesn't sound angry. He sounds like someone who has been given a present without a card.

n4.text: You play it four more times. Somewhere around the third the fog outside turns from grey to black, and you know you should go, and don't. On the fourth, Noah falls asleep against the wall with his head tipped back and his mouth slightly open, and the music ends in a hiss, and you realise you haven't heard anything else for an hour. When you move he stirs, looks at you, and then at the cold stove, the empty kettle. 'How long was I... did I...' You see him swallow. 'Did I say anything weird?'

wahl.label: 'You fell asleep. That's all.'
wahl.folge: He nods, and writes something on his wrist

wahl.label: 'You said you'd walk me to the road.'
wahl.folge: He goes pale, then thanks you

n5.text: 'Yes,' says Noah, 'yes, of course, it's dark soon.' He's already on his feet fussing with the kettle, the needle, the cord of the horn, anything. 'You shouldn't be out when the fog comes. It's NOT because of me, it's the road.' He wraps two cookies in a cloth and presses them into your hand with the movement you'd use to push somebody out of a burning room. At the door he hesitates. 'Next time I'll teach you the winding. It's not hard. You need a sort of rhythm.' He says it as if saying it were the guarantee.

wahl.label: Promise to come back
wahl.folge: He closes the door very softly

wahl.label: Wave and walk away
wahl.folge: You hear the first notes start again

n6.text: 'Don't be. I've never had anyone to play it for.' He winds the handle all thirty turns, slowly. 'I used to play it very quietly,' he says. 'Under the blanket. In case it woke somebody.' His mouth does something odd. 'There's nobody to wake now. That's what's strange. I keep waiting for someone to knock on the wall and say stop.' He puts the needle back on the first groove. 'Stay for one more?' It isn't a question, it's a small open door.

ort.gymnasium.k5.text: The Gymnasium is closed today, a handwritten sign on the door says GONE TO PRAY, BACK SOON, but the side door is open and the hallways are lit as if for an inspection. In the empty classroom the chairs stand in a perfect circle on the floor, and in the middle of the circle the globe, turned so the valley points at the ceiling. Someone stuck three pins in it, one in the town, one in the castle, one right where your house is, and from the three pins red threads run up to the lamp and meet in a knot.

optionen.name: Follow the threads to the lamp
optionen.text: The knot holds a photo, pinned in place: a grey-haired woman with a calm face, lying in a bed with her hands folded. Pinned beside it is a note: SHE WAITS. D.

optionen.name: Pull out one of the pins
optionen.text: The second the pin comes out, the hallway lights flicker, and somewhere on the second floor a locker door slams so hard the whole building hums.

varianten.beitritt: The Gymnasium door opens for you without a key, and the lamp in the classroom hangs just a bit lower than before, so the knot of red threads is at eye level. Connor's voice comes from the dark of the corridor, calm and quiet: 'You'll find what you need on the globe, friend. We left the pin in the castle for you.'

ort.haus.k5.text: When you come back to the house at dusk, the storm is rattling the windows, and the clean stripe on the floor has widened into a path that leads straight to the warm door, which now stands wide open. The circle in the room beyond it glows faintly in candlelight you did not light. You stand there for a long time without going in. The house is not angry. The house is PATIENT. It's waiting for you to bring something, you can feel it, the way you feel a cat staring at your hand when there's food in it.

optionen.name: Look at the circle on the floor
optionen.text: The scratches have been refreshed, deep and clean, and in the middle of the circle lies a flat round stone, polished smooth by years of something resting on it. Something about the size of a fist.

optionen.name: Go to bed early
optionen.text: You do. You sleep badly. Through the floor you can hear a faint, steady sound, tap, tap, tap, as if someone down there were patiently knocking to be let out.

varianten.tesserakt: The moment you cross the threshold with the cold in your pocket, every light in the house flickers once, and the warm door at the end of the hall swings wide on its own. The path on the floor glows faintly, as if somebody had walked it barefoot and wet. The house is no longer waiting. It's welcoming.

ort.lunuen.k5.text: The town is waiting. Thunder rolls over the roofs, and still every curtain is a fraction open and every candle a fraction brighter, and everyone you pass looks you straight in the face, the way people look at someone who is about to give a speech. Nobody speaks. A woman carries white flowers into the church. A man sweeps the same patch of pavement for the fifth time in the rain. The bakery has one loaf in the window and a little handwritten card next to it: FOR THE ONE WHO COMES BACK.

optionen.name: Take the loaf
optionen.text: Still warm, which makes no sense, and baked into the crust is a tiny iron nail wrapped in a scrap of paper with a child's drawing of a circle with three dots.

optionen.name: Walk into the church
optionen.text: Empty. The pews are polished and every brass plate is back in place, and the last plate on the last pew reads, in fresh engraving, your name.

varianten.beitritt: The loaf in the window is wrapped in a white cloth now, and the card says FOR OUR OWN. The baker opens the door before you reach it and hands you the loaf with both hands, as if it were a baby. 'You'll want to bring this with you,' she says softly. 'For the one downstairs.'

ort.nook.k5.text: The Nook looks the same to you as always, which is the creepiest part. The kettle is on, the cookies are on the table, the blanket is folded just right, and rain hammers the roof. Noah isn't here, but his scarf hangs over the back of his chair, and the cup next to it is still warm, so he can't be far. A pencil lies on an open page of the drawing book, and a new picture has been started: two figures in front of a big dark building, one small with a scarf, the other taller and taller, drawn so hard the pencil went through the paper.

optionen.name: Pick up the scarf
optionen.text: It's heavy and soft, and where it wraps around the neck the wool is rough and stained, like it has covered something for years. You put it back exactly where it was, because you can feel someone watching you do it.

optionen.name: Look at the drawing
optionen.text: Under the dark building he drew a square in the ground and in the square a tiny glowing shape. Next to it, in small print: HE WILL COME FOR IT. HE ALWAYS DOES.

varianten.tesserakt: The Nook is empty again, and the drawing in the book has changed. The tall figure in front of the castle has a small cube drawn in its hand now, in thick black crayon, and the small figure with the scarf is crossed out entirely. Under it: HE FOUND IT. HE ALWAYS DOES.

ort.schloss.k5.text: The castle sits on a rise at the edge of the valley, a black pile of stone with half its roof gone and ivy crawling in through every window, and tonight there's a storm coming, thunder walking around somewhere behind the hills. The iron gate stands open and the key from Connor's neck, or the one he gave you, or the one you found, fits the postern door without a sound. Inside, the air is cold and dry and it MOVES, very slightly, in and out, as if the ruin were breathing through a straw. On the ground floor one door is locked, and when you press your palm to it, it is warm, exactly as warm as a living body.

optionen.name: Press your hand against the warm locked door
optionen.text: Under your palm something moves, a slow dull thump, like a heart the size of a room. It beats twice, waits, beats again, faster, as if it noticed you. You take your hand away and the thumping stops, politely.

optionen.name: Search the east wing
optionen.text: A long hall with a collapsed ceiling, and at the end a library with most of the books rotted into black lumps. One shelf is clean. One shelf has no dust at all, and its books are lined up so precisely that you wonder if the shelf is actually a door.

optionen.name: Look out of a window at the valley
optionen.text: From up here the valley is laid out like a table setting: the town with its candle-lit windows, the lake like a grey coin, the hill with its black scar. All the paths lead here, you realise. Every single one.

varianten.beitritt: The postern door isn't just unlocked, it's open, and a trail of candles has been lit along the corridor floor all the way to the east wing. Someone has been here before you, quite recently, to make it nice. At the library entrance, a folded white cloth lies on the floor, set out for you to kneel on.
varianten.wiederbesuch: The castle again, and the warm door on the ground floor thumps twice as you pass, politely, like someone clearing their throat. The east wing shelf hangs open exactly as you left it. The stairs beyond are dark, and from the dark comes the faintest sound of someone humming.

ort.see.k5.text: For the first time the lake is perfectly calm even though a storm is coming. The fog has lifted and the water lies black and clear under a bruised sky, so still that the trees on the far shore stand upside down in it like a second forest. The playground is empty, the swing hangs motionless, and the double bench is empty too. On the seat lies one unlit cigarette on a folded napkin, with a single word on it in blue ballpoint: LATER. No birds, no insects, no wind. Even your footsteps seem to sink into the sand.

optionen.name: Pick up the cigarette
optionen.text: It's cold and smells of clove, and in the napkin there's a second note in a lazy hand: 'if you get what you want from down there, bring it HERE first. i'll hold it for you. promise. ~m'. You get the strange feeling that it's a joke, and that you are the joke.

optionen.name: Look into the water
optionen.text: For the first time you can see to the bottom, and the bottom is much too deep, a clear column of dark going down and down and down. Far below, something pale turns slowly and looks up.

varianten.beitritt: The cigarette on the bench is gone, and in its place there's a scrap of napkin with a single line in lazy blue ballpoint: you did it, didn't you. A pause. Under it, smaller: that's okay. i'm still here. The water ripples once, at the shore, right at your feet.
varianten.mika_hint: The napkin on the bench has more words on it this time. IT'S NOT LAKE-SHAPED. IT'S ME-SHAPED. WE'VE BEEN SHARING A BODY FOR A LONG TIME. The water below the bench has gone dark and perfectly still, and the reflection of the sky in it is the wrong colour, a deep wet red.

ort.wald.k5.text: The forest is darker than it should be at this hour and quiet the way a room is quiet after somebody said something unforgivable. Thin red cords have been strung from trunk to trunk around the path up the hill, a huge net, and from every cord hangs a tiny cloth doll with a button for a face. Nothing moves. Only after you pass the third one do you notice that all the dolls have turned, very slightly, to follow you with their blank eyes. Up the hill the black scar glows orange in the rain.

optionen.name: Touch one of the dolls
optionen.text: It's warm. Inside the little cloth body something ticks, regular, like a clock or a pulse. You let go and wipe your fingers on your coat until your hand stops feeling it.

optionen.name: Climb to the scorched patch
optionen.text: At the top, in the ash, there's a perfect circle of bare earth with one small wooden chair in the middle, charred black on one side and worn smooth on the other, facing the town.

varianten.tesserakt: The cold in your pocket makes the dolls turn faster. One by one, they swing around on their cords to face you, a hundred buttons for a hundred eyes, and the ticking inside them speeds up until it sounds like rain on a tin roof. On the hill the chair has turned to face the castle.

n1.text: There's a new sheet under the sugar tin, and it isn't headed WHEN I WOKE UP. It says, in his best handwriting with a ruler line under it: THINGS I WOULD LIKE TO DO IF I WERE NORMAL. Underneath, getting shakier toward the bottom: 1. Go to the lake in daylight and not check my hands. 2. Eat in the bakery, at the table. 3. Fall asleep and not be afraid of the morning. 4. Have somebody say my name from the other side of the room. 5. Play the record loud. Number 6 is only a number. Noah comes in with firewood and drops the whole armful when he sees you reading.

wahl.label: Say it's a lot of wishing for a hut

n2.text: He lets you get as far as number three. 'Stop. It's a dumb list.' He is on his knees among the logs, not picking them up. 'It's for after. If there's an after. Where I don't...' His mouth shuts. 'I've got a plan,' he says, flat and small, like somebody laying a coin on a counter to see whether it's enough. 'If you went away, I'd write. I'd have to learn the address. I think I could learn it.' He stands too quickly to get the wood back, and trips over the pile, and goes down on one knee with a log in each hand. 'I'm FINE,' he says, from the floor. 'Don't help. ...Hold this one.'

wahl.label: Hold the log, help him up
wahl.folge: He looks at you with terrible hope

n3.text: You slide it back under the tin exactly where it was, and he sees that you were careful. His shoulders come down an inch. He starts stacking logs, all with the bark facing the same way. 'I'm not normal,' he says to the woodpile, matter-of-fact. 'But it's good to have a list. You can cross things out. You can't cross out being scared.' A log rolls away and he catches it before it hits the floor. 'Number five's easy. The others are for later.' He glances at you, quick. 'I could do four with you. If you wanted. Just the name.'

wahl.label: Say his name from across the room
Say it's a good list
wahl.folge: He looks at you with terrible hope

n4.text: He sits among the logs and drags a shoebox from under the bench: tickets, drawings, a train map, a recipe for Linzer Torte with the quantities underlined twice. On the map a small careful circle on a town you've never heard of, with SOMEWHERE written in it. 'I'm very good at plans,' he says. 'I've got a whole box. People say things, and I plan around them, and then it doesn't happen and I have a plan with a hole in it.' Outside, on the road, someone's boots crunch the frost, slow and even. Noah's head turns toward the sound. 'You'd tell me, right? If it was never going to happen.'

n5.text: He writes it down. He takes the pencil and under number six, which had no words, writes in a tiny clear script: not far. He reads it back twice and underlines it so hard the line goes through the paper. 'That's the one thing I'd be able to keep. Not so far that I can't see the light.' He looks up, completely without sarcasm. 'I'll keep it on. In the evening. I keep it on anyway, for the foxes. But this time it would be for you, and I'd know, and it wouldn't be a lie.'

wahl.label: Say you'll look for it
wahl.folge: He nods, and nods, and doesn't stop

wahl.label: Take his hand
wahl.folge: His hand is cold, and he doesn't let go

n6.text: You say it from the doorway, across the whole width of the Nook, from the other side of the stove: 'Noah.' Just that. Not loud. He goes entirely still with a log in each hand, then turns round very slowly, the way you'd turn toward a sound you were afraid to frighten away. 'Again,' he says, almost inaudible. 'Please.' You say it again. And a third time, because he asks. On the third his face breaks without any noise, and he sits down on the floor with the logs in his lap. 'Okay. That's four. I'm crossing out four.' His hands shake so badly he can't hold the pencil, and you cross it out for him.

wahl.label: Give him back the pencil
wahl.folge: He holds it like a candle

wahl.label: Sit down on the floor with him
wahl.folge: He leans toward you, a quarter inch

n8.text: 'It's only paper.' He takes the sheet back and folds it very small and puts it in his sleeve, where the scarf and the scars are. 'It's just so I don't forget what ordinary looks like.' He puts the tea on, he stacks the logs with the bark facing the same way, he talks about the foxes and about frost on the road. He doesn't get angry and doesn't blush. All the little prickles that were his are put away somewhere, and it is a very clean, very polite afternoon. At the door he says, quickly, 'You can read the other one, if you come again,' and then shuts his mouth as if he had said too much.

wahl.label: Leave
wahl.folge: He closes the door and leans on it

n9.text: The knock comes soft, three times. Noah is on his feet before it ends, the lid is on the shoebox, the shoebox is under the bench, and he is standing in front of it with his arms at his sides, very straight, very calm. 'Behind the stove,' he says. The voice is level and low and nothing like his own. 'Quiet. Do not come out until I say.' He looks at you, and his eyes are pale and clear and entirely without fear, and his hand is shaking behind his back where he thinks you can't see it. Then he blinks, twice, and the boy is back, bewildered. 'Why am I... who's... go, hide, quick. Please.'

wahl.label: Stand next to him instead
wahl.folge: He shoves you gently, and he's strong

n10.text: It's only the wind. A branch, or the frost working at the latch, and the Nook is just a hut with a boy standing in it holding the poker. Noah looks at it, at the door, at you half-hidden behind the stove, and slowly lowers the poker. 'It's nothing,' he says. 'Nothing. I keep thinking...' He sits down. He pulls the sleeves over his knuckles. 'Whoever that was,' he says, 'just now, that wasn't me being rude. It's that I'm only brave when I'm scared enough.' He gives a laugh with no breath in it. 'Tomorrow,' he says. 'Come tomorrow. I'll make the good cookies. The ones without the burnt side.'

wahl.label: Say nothing and sit down beside him
wahl.folge: His shoulder is shaking against yours

n1.text: The east wing library smells of mold and cold stone, and the dust-free shelf stands against the end wall like a held breath. The books on it have blank spines, no titles, no numbers, but one sits a hair too far forward, a little crooked, like a tooth. When you step closer the draft that moves through the ruin seems to bend toward it, and you can hear, very faintly, another draft on the other side. 'You found a hidden door,' something in you says, quite calmly. 'Open it?'

n2.text: The shelf swings inward on a silent hinge, and cold air slides out, smelling of earth and iron and something sweet and old. Beyond it a narrow spiral stair goes down into complete blackness, its steps worn into shallow dips by centuries of feet. Your phone light only reaches the first dozen. The silence down there is not empty. It is the kind of silence a big animal keeps when it's lying very still.

wahl.label: Go down
wahl.folge: The player enters the cellar (see the next scene)

n3.text: You push the book back flush with the others and the draft stops, the way a held breath stops when you finally let it out. For a moment you're relieved. Then, behind the shelf, something taps three times. Slow. Patient. Not angry. Just reminding you that the door is still there, and that you're the one who can open it.

wahl.label: Leave the library
wahl.folge: The door remains closed until the player returns

n4.text: Three knocks, hollow, against the wood. You wait. Four seconds pass. Then, from behind the shelf, from low down, about knee height, someone knocks back. Three times. Exactly the same rhythm. Then two more, a half-beat off, like someone who is learning the pattern. The book on the shelf has moved forward by itself while you were listening.

varianten.beitritt: The book on the shelf is already sticking out when you enter. Someone has slipped a white cloth under it so you won't scratch the wood, and there's a fresh candle burning on the floor. A tiny tag hangs from the spine: FOR OUR NEW MEMBER, WITH LOVE.

n1.text: The cellar is not a cellar. It's a room that has forgotten the rules of rooms. The ceiling is too high, then too low, the walls meet at angles that make your eyes ache, and all the sound is gone: your footsteps, your breath, your own pulse in your ears, as if you'd stepped under glass. A heavy beam crosses the ceiling, its middle worn smooth in the shape of a rope. And beneath it, floating at the height of your chest, turns something you can't hold in your head, a cube inside a cube inside a cube, each a different colour of dark. It's cold. It's wrong. It's looking at you. 'A weird tesseract-looking artifact floats in the middle of the room,' something says. 'Take it?'

n2.text: It's like picking up a stone that isn't there. For a long second your fingers close around nothing, then the weight arrives all at once, ice-cold, heavy as a drowned thing, and your hand fills with a sound you can't hear. In that sound a boy's voice speaks, small and young and very far away: 'Don't. Please don't. I didn't mean to touch it.' Then it's gone. The cube settles in your palm, humming against your bones, and the room lets out a long slow sigh, like something that waited a long time and can finally exhale.

wahl.label: Carry it up the stairs
wahl.folge: The Tesseract is now in the player's inventory

n3.text: You back away one slow step at a time, and the shape turns to follow you, patient, unhurried, as if it understood. At the stairs you look back. It's still there, still turning, and it's the only thing in the room that casts no shadow. Your hands are shaking. You realise you could leave right now, and maybe you should. And you realise, as you take the stairs two at a time, that it's already too late for that. It knows your face.

wahl.label: Climb the stairs
wahl.folge: The player returns later or never; Noah's strength stays at base

n4.text: You look up at the beam. The wood is worn into a smooth hollow right where a rope would hang, and in the dust below, directly under it, lies a crumbling scrap of cloth the colour of old bone. You don't want to think about whose it was. A hundred centuries of silence press on your eardrums. Without the sound, the cube seems to listen harder. It has turned, just slightly, so that one of its faces looks directly at you.

k5.draussen.text: You step out of the castle with the cold weight in your jacket, and the storm finally breaks, big cold drops hammering the ruin. Halfway down the hill road you feel it, a prickle on the back of your neck, the sense of someone walking behind you at exactly your pace, and when you stop, the footsteps stop half a second later. You turn around slowly. At the far end of the road, at the edge of a lightning flash, a small shape stands beside a tree in a scarf that is much too big for him. Your pocket has gone icy. Whatever is in there, he is drawn to it like a moth, and as you watch, his silhouette flickers, shrinks, grows, shrinks again, as if two different people were trying to wear the same coat.

varianten.tesserakt: The cold in your jacket grows with every step. On the road behind you, the footsteps have a second rhythm now, a heavier one, a step that doesn't belong to the boy. When you glance back, the small figure beside the tree is standing very still, and his shadow on the wet road is twice his height.

ort.gymnasium.k6.text: The Gymnasium is back to being an ordinary Tuesday, bells and shoes and the roar of a hundred kids at lunch. Nobody looks at you twice, and when you check the classroom with the globe and the red threads, it's just a classroom, tidy, bright, with a wall calendar and a slightly overwatered plant. The threads are gone. The pins are gone. There's only a small clean hole in the globe where your house stands, and a drawing pinned to the board by some kid: a circle with three dots, in green crayon.

optionen.name: Ask a teacher about the drawing
optionen.text: 'Oh, that's just a game they invented,' she says brightly. 'They call it The Keeper. The loser has to stand in the middle and not move. Isn't that sweet?'

optionen.name: Look at the school photos by the entrance
optionen.text: All back to normal, every face. Only in the oldest one, from the seventies, you spot the boy in the scarf again, small, smiling, and a hand resting on his shoulder from just outside the frame.

varianten.traum: After the dream, the Gymnasium smells faintly of plaster. In the cleaned classroom you find, on the teacher's desk, a tiny lump of wet grey mud, as if someone had carried it in on a shoe. The globe has a small clean hole at the spot where your house stands, exactly the size of a fingertip.

ort.haus.k6.text: The house is quiet now, the way a guest is quiet when they've finally been asked to sit. Sunlight pours through every window, bright and warm and wrong, and with the cold cube in your pocket the smell is almost gone. The warm door is closed, and it's just wood. The clean stripe on the floor leads to your own feet and stops. In the kitchen the cup is full and steaming, and next to it stands a second cup that was not there this morning, with lipstick on the rim.

optionen.name: Set the cube on the kitchen table
optionen.text: It sits there without a sound, still turning, a tiny cold star of dark. Every light in the house dims at once and comes back brighter, and in the hall the warm door clicks open by itself.

optionen.name: Go to bed with the cube in your pocket
optionen.text: You lie down in your clothes. The sheets smell of soap and smoke. You close your eyes, and the whole house closes its eyes with you, and somewhere deep in the walls a lot of very small things begin to hum.

varianten.traum: The wall at knee height in the warm room has a long clean crack in it now, running from floor to ceiling, and you can't remember whether you did that or the dream did. Your fingers are still stiff, as if they had been inside something. The cup in the kitchen is full of warm tea, and the second one has a lipstick ring.
varianten.tesserakt: You hold the cube tight in your pocket as you cross the threshold, and for the first time the house doesn't react at all. No hum, no warm door, no dripping. It is the stillness of a held breath, of something that has been waiting a hundred years and knows it can wait one more night.

ort.lunuen.k6.text: In the morning the town acts as if nothing happened, and that is so exactly right it makes your teeth hurt. The sun is out, a thin false gold on the wet roofs, the baker waves, the man at the bus stop nods like an old friend, and kids walk to school in pairs, and for the first time you notice that they are holding hands. Nobody mentions the dream, because nobody knows about the dream. You walk down the main street with a cold weight in your pocket and a hundred friendly faces and you have never in your life felt so observed.

optionen.name: Greet the baker back
optionen.text: 'Sleep well, dear?' she asks and slides a pastry across the counter. 'The first night after a long trip is always the strangest.' You didn't tell her about a trip. You say yes. You eat the pastry. It tastes of nothing.

optionen.name: Look up at the church windows
optionen.text: Someone in a dark cardigan stands in the middle window, hands in his sleeves, looking down at you with an expression of such tender patient love that you'd have to look away if you could.

varianten.traum: Everyone in town acts like they didn't see your face last night. The baker has something sweet ready before you ask, and the man at the bus stop tips an imaginary hat. A child on the pavement looks up at you, then at your hands, and says very clearly, 'You smell like inside.' Then her mother pulls her away.

ort.nook.k6.text: The Nook is warm and quiet. Noah sits in his chair with a book he isn't reading and the blanket pulled up to his chin, and when you come in his whole face lights up as if someone flipped a switch. 'Oh! You're here! Not that I... you know. It's just, I made too many cookies again.' He seems completely normal, which, you realise, is its own kind of terrifying. He doesn't know what you did last night. He doesn't know what's in your pocket. Only once, when you reach for a cookie, his eyes flick to your jacket and stay there a half-second too long.

optionen.name: Ask him how he slept
optionen.text: 'Fine!' he says, too fast. 'I had a weird dream, but I don't remember it. There were lots of people in my house, and they were all looking up at me.' He laughs. 'Funny, right? I don't even have an upstairs.'

optionen.name: Give him a cookie back
optionen.text: He takes it like it's the most precious thing anyone has ever given him and eats it very slowly with his eyes closed, as if he's afraid it might be taken away.

varianten.tesserakt: Noah pulls the blanket up to his eyes when you step in, and his smile is wobbly. 'You're carrying something,' he says. 'I can feel it from here. It makes my teeth ache.' He laughs, nervous. 'Obviously it's none of my business. But if you're going to put it down, could you put it down somewhere that isn't here?'

ort.schloss.k6.text: You didn't mean to come here, and yet your feet brought you, as they do now. In the false sunlight the castle is a hollow, glittering shell with swallows in the broken rafters, and none of it feels honest. The warm door on the ground floor is not warm today, it's just a door. The shelf in the east wing hangs open on its hinges and the stairs beyond are empty and silent. And still you can feel the cellar looking up at you. It misses what you took. It has been very patient. It will not be patient forever.

optionen.name: Look down the stairs
