optionen.text: The dark at the bottom is not still. It moves slowly in and out, like a sleeper's chest, and when you lean forward it pulls back by exactly the distance you moved.

optionen.name: Look at the stone above the doorway
optionen.text: A line of old lettering you can't read, a circle with three dots after it, and below it, newer, scratched in with a nail: HE WILL BRING IT BACK.

varianten.tesserakt: The cold in your pocket leans toward the castle like a compass needle. Inside the ruin, the east wing shelf is already open, and the thump from the warm door on the ground floor beats in time with your heart. The cellar, you realise, isn't calling you back. It's reeling you in.

ort.see.k6.text: The lake is a postcard. Sun on the water, ducks that actually quack, a child on the swing, a mother with a stroller, everything so perfect it looks painted. The double bench is occupied. Mika sits on it with his arms along the backrest and his face tilted up to the sun, glowing like a cat in a sunbeam, grinning at nothing. As you come closer you hear that he's humming a lazy, cheerful tune, over and over, and it takes you a moment to realise that you know it, because you dreamt it last night.

optionen.name: Greet him
optionen.text: 'Heyyy,' he says, and the word has a hundred extra letters in it. 'Look at you. All shiny. Slept well?' He is the happiest you have ever seen him. He is too happy. And the sun doesn't reach his eyes.

optionen.name: Watch the children on the playground
optionen.text: The child on the swing swings in a perfect rhythm with the exact same smile, and the mother pushes without looking at the child, her eyes fixed on the bench. On Mika. She's smiling too.

varianten.mika_hint: Mika looks at you over his shoulder and he is smiling so brightly that the sun in the lake looks dull. 'Look at that,' he says. 'You figured it out, didn't you? Not the whole thing. Just the shape of it.' He pats the bench. 'Sit. I'll let you ask me one question, and I won't lie. I never do. I just might answer a different one.'

ort.wald.k6.text: In daylight the forest could almost be nice. Sun slants through the red and gold leaves, a woodpecker works a trunk, and the scratched circles look like ordinary tree scars, nothing more. It would be easy to forget what you saw here, and that's the trick of it, you realise, the way everything in this valley gives you permission to forget. At the top of the black scar the little chair is still there, its charred side facing the town, and somebody has left a fresh white flower on the seat with its stem tied in a neat knot.

optionen.name: Smell the flower
optionen.text: It has no smell at all. When you pick it up the knot unties itself, the stem uncurls and the petals turn grey and crumble in your hand like ash.

optionen.name: Sit in the chair
optionen.text: It's too small for you, and warm, as if whoever sat in it just left. From here you see the whole valley, and for a moment you understand why anyone would sit here: to watch over what they were trying to protect.

varianten.traum: After the dream the forest feels different, like a room whose furniture has been moved. The flower on the chair is gone and the chair has been turned around, so it faces the ridge now instead of the town. A few steps away, in the leaves, there's a small clean footprint. It's pointed toward your house.

n1.text: The Nook is spotless when you come in, scrubbed so hard that the planks have gone pale, the stove polished, and on the table, in a row like a still life, stand two cups, a blue one with a fox and a small wooden one with your name. Noah is on the crate, hands pressed between his knees, the scarf wound twice. 'I cleaned. NOT because... I had time.' He gets up. 'Sit, please. I want to do it right. I've been practising for nine days. I'll do it now, before the day has a hole in it.'

n2.text: He puts his hands at his sides, straight as a boy in front of a class, and looks at a spot just past your left ear. 'Thank you,' says Noah, slowly, every syllable its own thing, 'for the cup. For sitting down. For not asking why I wash it. For the stone that sank.' His voice shakes once, on stone. 'For saying my name from the other side of the room. I didn't know it could sound like that. I thought it was just something people used to get my attention.' He stops. 'It doesn't sound weird,' he says, with wonder. 'It doesn't sound weird at all.'

n3.text: 'I do,' says Noah. 'I have to.' He's already pouring, his hands much too steady. 'Because if I don't say it now, there might be a day coming.' He sets the kettle down and doesn't look at you. 'You'd tell me, right? If it was that day. If I'd done something. You wouldn't let me find out from someone else. You'd say it straight out. And you'd be kind, but you'd say it.' He asks it in the voice of someone asking for a glass of water. His fingers on the cup are white at the tips.

wahl.label: 'I'd tell you. I promise.'
wahl.folge: He lets out all his air

wahl.label: 'Nothing is going to happen to you.'
wahl.folge: He smiles, and it's the saddest thing you've seen

n4.text: You say it all back, the cup and the stone and the name, and it comes out clumsier than his, because you haven't practised, and halfway you realise that's why he did. He listens with his whole face, like rain on a roof after a drought. When you finish he nods once, formally, like a man accepting a document. Then he sits down on the crate as if his knees were cut, and the scarf slips off one shoulder, and he doesn't fix it. 'Okay,' he says. 'That's done. I got to say it.' He smiles at the cup. 'Whatever else happens, that's done.'

wahl.label: Drink the tea with him
wahl.folge: The Nook is quiet and warm

wahl.label: Hold the scarf out to him
wahl.folge: He lets you wind it back on

n5.text: His hand is a small cold bundle of bones in yours, the scar tissue smooth along the back of it, and he doesn't pull away. He looks at it as if it belonged to someone else. 'Warm,' he says. 'I forgot hands were warm.' He holds on harder, with hardly any strength, as though trying to remember it for later. 'If it's bad,' he whispers, 'if the day has a hole in it and you're there, and you're scared of me, you have to say. It's not rude. It's the opposite.'

wahl.label: 'I'll say. I won't be scared of you.'
wahl.folge: He lets out all his air

wahl.label: 'I'll stay.'
wahl.folge: He smiles, and it's the saddest thing you've seen

n6.text: 'Good,' he says. 'That's good.' He nods as though handed the last piece of a very large puzzle and trying not to look at the picture. He pours, gives you the wooden cup with your name and keeps the blue one, and for a while you drink in a silence so peaceful it frightens you a little. 'I put the drawing of the two cups up,' he says. 'Behind you.' You turn. It's pinned over the door, between the clean nail and the knothole shaped like a mouth: two cups side by side, and under them in his careful hand, THE ONES WHO STAYED.

wahl.label: Finish the tea with him
wahl.folge: The fire burns low and gold

n7.text: His smile is slow and absolutely unprotected, a smile with the lid off. 'That's what everyone says,' says Noah, not unkindly. 'It's the right thing to say.' He turns the blue cup, and the painted fox turns with it. 'But if there's a day when it isn't true, would you promise me one thing?' He waits for you to nod. 'Make it quick. And make sure it's you. Nobody else. Not him. You.' It sits between you, absurdly polite, absurdly plain, a boy asking a favour as though asking you to hold his place in a line.

wahl.label: 'I can't promise that.'
wahl.folge: He says 'okay' and means it, and it's worse

wahl.label: 'Drink your tea, Noah.'
wahl.folge: He drinks, and doesn't ask again

n1.text: You open your eyes and you're still in bed, same ceiling, same window, but the light is wrong, a warm yellow flicker coming up through the floorboards, and from downstairs there's a murmur of voices, a lot of them, low and steady like a congregation. You try to sit up and you weigh NOTHING. Your hand goes straight through the blanket. You're a ghost in your own house, and whatever is happening in the kitchen, it's happening a hundred years ago. The cube in your pocket isn't in your pocket anymore, but somehow you can still feel it, like a cold finger on the back of your neck, saying: go and look.

wahl.label: Stay in the bed and wait it out
wahl.folge: The dream drags you down anyway

n2.text: The kitchen is full of people in dark coats standing in a ring around the table, and on the table lies a small bundle in a cloth. At the head stands a thin, hard-faced woman with folded hands, and you know her at once from the photo in the tin: young Lizzy. 'Not this time either,' she says. A man with a candle unwraps the cloth. A baby, blue-grey, too still, eyes shut forever. The ring lets out one sigh from twelve mouths. 'Into the fire,' says Lizzy, and they pick the bundle up and carry it down the hall to the warm door, and you realise this is not the first time they've done this. Not the second. Not the tenth.

wahl.label: Follow them to the warm room
wahl.folge: You see what the cult did

wahl.label: Try to touch the man with the candle

n3.text: The bed tilts like a boat. You slide, without any fear, through the mattress, through the floor, through the kitchen ceiling, and land on your feet in the ring of dark coats. Nobody looks at you. A small bundle lies on the table. At the head stands young Lizzy, and for exactly one heartbeat her eyes find yours, calm, tired, as if she had been expecting you for years. Then she nods toward the hall, and the ring opens like a mouth.

wahl.label: Go through the ring
wahl.folge: You see what the cult did

n4.text: The warm room is lit by a circle of candles, and the bundle is laid in the middle of the scratched circle on the floor. They sing, quiet and ordinary, almost a lullaby, while a man brings a bucket of wet plaster and a trowel. And then they wall it in. One trowel at a time, a layer of grey mud over the little face, over the cloth, smoothing it flat, until it's only a slightly newer patch in the old wall. It doesn't take long. That's the worst part. The crying is the only thing that takes time, and every single one of them is crying while they do it, and none of them stops.

n5.text: Your hand goes through the man with the candle like through smoke, and the flame gutters. He frowns, almost looks at you, then shakes it off. But at the head of the table the woman slowly turns her head, and looks at the empty space where you are standing. 'Someone is here,' says young Lizzy, to the room. 'Someone from after.' She isn't afraid. She smiles, thin and sad and determined, and says one more word that you can't hear, and then the whole ring turns toward the hall, and she walks, and you follow, because the dream pulls you like a leash.

wahl.label: Follow them to the warm room
wahl.folge: You see what the cult did

n6.text: She doesn't follow the others. She stays at the table, alone, her hands trembling now that nobody's looking, and she opens a drawer and takes out a small square of paper and a pencil stub and writes in cramped little letters, pressing so hard the point breaks. When she's done she folds the paper in four, and then in eight, and puts it into her apron. 'For whoever comes after,' she says, to the empty kitchen, not to you, or maybe to you. 'Please read it. Please be better than we were.' Then she follows the others, and the candle on the table burns down by an inch while you stand there and cannot move.

wahl.label: Follow her to the warm room
wahl.folge: You see what the cult did

n7.text: The dream jumps like a skipped tape. It's later. The room is empty, the candles are stubs, and young Lizzy kneels alone in front of the patched wall, crying without any sound. She takes a metal pick from her apron and carves a thin line into the fresh plaster, just deep enough, reaches in and tilts the wall open like a little door. Behind it lies the newest baby, grey and perfect and still whole. She puts the folded paper in its mouth, gently, as a mother feeds a child, and whispers: 'For when someone finally comes who can read.' Then she presses the plaster closed with her thumb, smooths it, and kisses the spot.

n8.text: You run at them, you scream, you throw yourself at the man with the trowel, and you pass through all of them like through a stack of cold sheets. Nobody turns. The mud goes on, and the singing goes on, and the little face disappears under the grey, and all your shouting is just a draft in the room. You hit the floor on your knees, sobbing, and the floorboards are WARM under your hands, warm and slightly soft, like skin, and a voice from very far below the house says, tenderly, 'Shh. It's only a dream. Watch.'

n9.text: You wake up in your bed, in the dark, in your own body, your heart hammering in your throat. The cube lies on the pillow, cold and still. Without deciding to, you get up, go down the stairs and into the warm room, and put your palm against the patch in the wall, exactly at knee height. It's warm. It's waiting. Do you tear it open?

wahl.label: Yes, reach into its mouth
wahl.folge: You try to get the note

n11.text: You push two fingers between the cold lips, and the skin gives like wet paper, and you feel the edge of something dry and folded, far back in the throat, out of reach. You hook for it. The tiny jaw snaps shut on your finger with a click, not a bite, a reflex, you tell yourself, a REFLEX, and when you wrench free the tip of your finger stays behind between its gums. Blood runs down your wrist. The paper is still in there. The body is warm. You know what you have to do.

wahl.label: Pull the jaw apart with your hands
Take the note and run
wahl.folge: The player has the note: see the next scene

wahl.label: Take the note and run
wahl.folge: The player has the note: see the next scene

n14.text: You stand with your hand on the warm wall for a long time. Then you take it away. The house sighs, with disappointment or relief, you can't tell, and the lights go out one by one up the stairs. In the morning there's a stain on your palm that doesn't wash off, and the cube on the pillow has not moved. Whatever the wall is keeping, it's still keeping it. But you know now that it's there, and sooner or later you won't be able to stop thinking about it.

wahl.label: Get up
wahl.folge: The note stays hidden; the player must find another way later

k6.zettel.text: The paper is yellowed and thin as onion skin, in a cramped upright hand that you recognise from the tin in the kitchen. Part one: 'Whoever finds this, the lake is not a lake. It was here before the town and will be here after. The people think they are feeding it. It lets them. It is bored, and a bored thing is more dangerous than an angry one. It will show itself to you, and it will be charming. Do not trust the help it gives. It cannot lie, but it can leave things out.' Part two, on the back, in smaller letters: 'D. is dead, but something took her body and wears it still, in the stone room beneath the castle, beside the Door. It is what the boy let in when he touched the Cube. It sleeps. It is sleeping in HIM. If the Cube is brought near it, it wakes. Put the Cube back where it belongs, before it is too late. And forgive me, whoever you are. I should have burned this house to the ground.'

n1.text: Mika is on the bench in the evening light, humming, and the humming stops the second you step onto the grass. 'There you are,' he says with a bright, shining joy. 'Man, I was HOPING you'd come by. Sit, sit.' He pats the bench with both hands. He looks younger. His eyes are clear and wet and shining, like a kid's on his birthday. 'You look tired. Rough night? You know, I had the weirdest dream. There was this house, and a bunch of people in a kitchen, and someone watching from the stairs...' He grins. 'I'm not gonna tell you who. That'd spoil it.'

wahl.label: Ask if he knows what was in the wall

n2.text: He laughs, clear and clean, and rests his chin on his fist. 'I like you. I really do. I think I haven't liked anyone in a long time. Everybody else is so predictable.' He squints at the lake. 'You know what's funny? You're the first one in a hundred years who tore open the wall. Most of them just stare at it. They put flowers there. You just ripped it right open.' A thin glittering ripple runs through his hair, like water. 'That's lovely. That's SO lovely. Thank you.'

wahl.label: Say you didn't do it for him
wahl.folge: Mika's laugh is a bit too long

n3.text: 'What was in the wall?' He tastes the words. 'Oh, man. Everything they were ever afraid of. Everything they thought would keep them safe.' He leans closer and the smell of cloves is overwhelming. 'It's all just meat. You know that now. All their prayers, all their sad little candles, meat in a wall. And it was never me they were feeding. They thought it was. I let them.' He pulls back and the warm, lazy charm is back. 'Anyway! Don't mind me. I'm just high.'

n4.text: He takes the note carefully with two fingers and holds it up to the light. His lips move as he reads. By the second part he is smiling so wide his eyes crinkle shut. 'Lizzy,' he sighs fondly. 'God, she was a pain. She never trusted me. Smart woman.' He hands it back. 'Everything she says is true, by the way. Every word. The part she leaves out is that I never lie.' He lights a fresh cigarette. 'Left or right, man. You still never told me. Which way around the lake?'

n5.text: He waves you off with a lazy flick of his fingers. 'Go on. You've got a place to be. A basement. A boy. Someone's waiting.' He leans back, closes his eyes and goes back to humming that same happy tune, and as you walk away the humming gets louder instead of quieter, until the whole shore is humming with him, every blade of grass, every ripple on the water, one single cheerful note.

wahl.label: Leave the lake
wahl.folge: The player is ready for the finale

varianten.mika_hint: He doesn't even look at you when you step onto the grass. 'You can ask me now,' says Mika, still facing the water. 'I've been waiting for you to ask. It's been a hundred years. Anything.' He draws on his cigarette. 'But think before you do. Some questions have answers you can't give back.'
varianten.beitritt: 'Oh,' says Mika, and the sun goes out of his voice like a candle in a draft. 'You joined them. After all of that.' He puts his cigarette out against the bench very carefully, a long slow twist. 'Fine. Fine, man. It's your life.' A beat. 'Sit anyway. I want to see what they did to you.'

n1.text: The Nook is dark except for one candle, and the stove is cold for the second time since you met him. Noah sits on the floor in front of an old record player with the blanket over his shoulders, and the speaker crackles like a fire before the piano comes in, slow, soft, one note and then another like somebody carefully setting down glass. He doesn't turn around. 'Sit,' he says. 'Don't talk during the good part. It's NOT like I want you here, I just... didn't want to listen to it alone, okay?'

wahl.label: Sit down next to him on the floor

n2.text: You sit, and the floorboards are warm from the stove he lit earlier, and for a minute neither of you says anything. The piece swells and falls back like water in the dark. Noah pulls his knees up and rests his chin on them. 'Clair de Lune,' he says, finally, very quietly. 'Moonlight. It's the only thing in this whole valley that doesn't want anything from me.' A pause. 'My mom hated it. She said it was...' He stops, mid-word, and his face goes smooth, and then he laughs a small laugh. 'Anyway.'

wahl.label: Ask about his mom
wahl.folge: Noah goes cold for a moment

n3.text: 'THAT'S MY CHAIR, IDIOT!' He's half up before he realises you've seen his face, and his cheeks go red as the candle, and he sits back down, in front of your knees instead, with his back against your shins, as if that was the plan the whole time. 'Fine. Whatever. Stay. It's more comfortable than the floor anyway. NOT that I'd say that out loud.' The piano goes on. Somewhere in the second minute you feel his shoulders drop an inch, and then another.

wahl.label: Ask about his mom
wahl.folge: Noah goes cold for a moment

n4.text: 'Debussy. French. Dead.' He says it like a joke and then ruins it by smiling. 'It's the one thing from before that I kept. I found the record in a box and the box was the only box nobody burned.' He winces, as if the word had a taste. 'I mean, threw away. Whatever. Sit down, you're blocking the light.' You sit. The candle flame leans toward the speaker as if it were listening too.

n5.text: 'We don't talk about her.' Not Noah's voice. Even, polite, very adult, and the candle flame stands up straight as if someone had pulled it by the head. Then the room breathes out and he's small again, hands over his mouth. 'Sorry. Sorry! That was... I don't know where that came from. Sometimes things come out of my mouth and I wasn't the one who sent them.' He laughs, thin and awful. 'Please don't look at me like that. I like it when you look at me normal.'

wahl.label: Apologise and say you don't have to say anything

n6.text: The piece slows down, the last third, where the notes stretch out like a hand reaching. Noah is very still. 'Can I tell you something stupid?' he says. 'Sometimes I lose time. I wake up and my hands are cold and the kettle is still warm, and I don't remember putting it on.' He is looking straight at the candle. 'If I ever... if I ever did something. Would you tell me? Even if it's bad. Even if I'd hate you for it. I'd rather know.'

wahl.label: Promise him, no matter what
wahl.folge: Noah's trust is at its peak

wahl.label: Tell him you're scared too, and you'll tell him anyway
wahl.folge: Noah's trust is at its peak

wahl.label: Make a joke to lighten it
wahl.folge: Noah laughs, a little too loud

n7.text: His fingers are ice at first, thin and shaking, and then they close around yours hard enough to hurt. 'Your hands are warm,' he whispers. 'Mine never are. Isn't that weird? I make so much tea.' He turns your hand over and looks at it as if it were a letter he can't read. 'Nobody ever just... held it. They always wanted it to do something.' The piano is almost gone. 'Idiot,' he says, and it's the softest word you've ever heard.

n8.text: 'Okay,' he says. 'Okay.' It's barely a sound. He lets his head fall against your shoulder, and the weight of it is so small that it frightens you. 'I'm not going to sleep,' he mumbles. 'I'm just going to rest my eyes during the last part.' The needle reaches the end of the record and starts to whisper in the groove, round and round. Noah is breathing slow and even against your neck. And then, from very deep inside his sleep, in a flat quiet voice that is not his, he says: 'He likes you too. That's the problem.' His fingers curl around your sleeve. You don't move until the candle goes out.

wahl.label: Stay until the candle is out
wahl.folge: Noah's bond with the player is deep

n9.text: He laughs a beat too loudly, then covers it with his sleeve. 'Right! Yes! It'll definitely be fine, haha.' The joke sits on the floor between you and nobody picks it up. The record reaches its last bars, and the needle starts to whisper in the groove, round and round, and Noah gets up to lift it, very carefully, with both hands. 'It's late, idiot,' he says, back turned. 'Go home. I mean... it was nice. NOT that it matters.' The candle is already smoking when you reach the door.

wahl.label: Go home
wahl.folge: Noah is a little more alone

ort.schloss.k7.text: You bring the cube back because the paper in your pocket told you to, because the cold in your coat has become unbearable, and because the whole valley seems to lean toward the castle as you climb the hill. It's night, dead silent, no wind, no rain, not even an insect. The gate is open, the postern door is open, the shelf in the east wing is folded back like an open mouth, and the stairs going down are no longer dark. A thin orange light comes up them, with the sweet smell of the house, and a sound: slow, wet, patient. Someone down there is breathing very carefully, on purpose.

optionen.name: Look down the stairs
optionen.text: At the bottom of the spiral you can see the orange glow and a long shadow across the floor, the shadow of someone standing quite still. It's much too tall. While you watch, it shrinks to the size of a child, then stretches again, like breathing.

optionen.name: Check behind you
optionen.text: A small figure stands in the library doorway, scarf trailing, hands clasped in front of him as if in prayer. He followed you. He has followed you the whole way. 'I-I wasn't!' says Noah, and then: 'Please don't go down there.'

varianten.tesserakt: You walk up the hill with the cube so cold against your ribs that you feel it in your teeth. The gate swings open before you touch it. The castle doesn't breathe in and out anymore. It holds its breath. Down in the cellar, something has heard you coming, and it is smiling.

k7.anreise.text: The stairs go down and down, turning on themselves, until you can't tell if you're descending into the earth or into the memory of a place. The cube in your coat is so cold it hurts. Halfway down you hear his footsteps behind you, quick, light, anxious, hurrying to catch up and stopping a moment too far back. You don't turn around. 'Hey,' says Noah's voice, small and breathless. 'Hey. Wait. I just wanted to... I don't know why I came. It's not like I want to be here. It's just that you looked like you were walking to your own funeral, and I thought, somebody should be there. Even if it's mine.'

n1.text: The cellar is exactly as you remember it: the wrong angles, the dead air, the beam above. On the floor under the beam nothing floats at all, only a flat grey stone and a hole in the world where something is missing. Against the far wall, half in shadow, lies a long dry shape on a slab, a figure in rotted white with grey hair spread out like roots and cupped hands on its chest, and the shape is breathing. Noah has stopped beside you. His eyes are fixed on your coat. 'You brought it back,' he whispers. 'Oh no, you brought it BACK. You don't understand. I touched it when I was little, and I woke up in my bed and everyone said it was a dream, but it was never a dream, and now he's...' His voice cracks. 'Please. Please help me. I don't know how to say it. I never learned how to say it.'

wahl.label: Take his hand
wahl.folge: Noah's trust is at its peak

wahl.label: Put the cube down on the stone

n2.text: His hand is ice cold and shaking, and he grips yours with both of his, fiercely, like a child at the dentist's. 'Thank you. Thank you, thank you.' He's smiling and tears are pouring down his face. 'It's not like I wanted to ask. I really never do.' He looks at you, calm and clear for a moment. 'If it gets bad, don't believe what I say. Not the loud one. Not the quiet one. Not the other one.' He glances over his shoulder at the slab. 'Not any of us.' His grip tightens until it hurts. 'I'm so sorry. He's already awake.'

wahl.label: Hold on to him
wahl.folge: The boss intro starts: wrong line for Noah

n3.text: 'Him,' says Noah. 'The one who watches. The one who laughs.' The cheerful voice is gone, replaced by something thin and flat and old. 'I see everything he does. Every person. Every night. I see it with his eyes and I can't look away, and I can't tell anyone, because then they'll hurt me again, and when I'm hurt he gets hungry, and when he's hungry...' He claps both hands over his mouth and shakes his head, and the bright smile snaps back like a trap. 'I mean! Nothing! Forget it! It's not like I said anything!' The smile does not reach the rest of his face. It never will again.

wahl.label: Take his hand
wahl.folge: Noah's trust is at its peak

n4.text: You lower the cube toward the stone and the whole room tilts. Every shadow bends toward it, and the air drops ten degrees. The figure on the slab sits up in one smooth movement, hands falling apart, head lolling, with the dry creak of a very old chair. Noah screams, a short high surprised sound, folds in half and clutches his skull. 'No, no, he's up, he's coming, I can feel him, STOP IT, I'M NOT, I'M NOT, I'M NOT...' When he straightens, his face is completely smooth. 'Hello,' says Noah, politely. 'Thank you for bringing it.'

wahl.label: Step back
wahl.folge: The boss intro starts: wrong choice

n5.text: 'The one who hurts,' he says, in the same flat voice. 'He's not a person. He's just everything that happened, finally allowed to stand up.' He rubs his sleeve over his eyes. 'The cube lets him out. It always did. That's why Connor wants it near me.' His voice drops to almost nothing. 'Don't let him have it. Don't let me have it. Whatever I say.'

wahl.label: Hold on to him
wahl.folge: The boss intro starts: before the boss

n6.text: He looks at you for a long time. Then his shoulders drop, the cheerful tension drains out of his face, and what is left is beautiful and calm and without any warmth. 'I see.' Even his voice has changed, lighter, kinder, almost gentle. 'You were going to leave him alone with this. They always do.' He tilts his head. 'It's alright. I'll take it from here.' And he holds out his hand, palm up, for the cube.

wahl.label: Hold on to the cube
wahl.folge: The boss intro starts: before the boss

varianten.tesserakt: The cube in your coat is so cold the cloth has frosted over. Noah stops three steps behind you, his face white. 'It's loud,' he says. 'It's so loud, I can't hear myself. Can you hear it? It's saying my name. It's saying all of them.' His voice splits down the middle on the last word, one half high and bright, the other half low and very calm.

n1.text:
Noah kneels in the middle of the cellar floor, small, wet, shaking. Blood has dried on his cheeks in stripes. The dry woman beside him has crumbled to dust. The cube lies on the stone, quiet, and for a moment the cellar has ordinary angles again.

(His head lifts. His eyes, for the first time all night, are clear and blue and young.)

NOAH: It's done? Is he gone?

(His hand reaches for yours.)

NOAH: Please don't hurt me. Please, I'll be good, I'll be so good. I'll make you tea every day, I promise, please.

And behind his eyes, a long way back, something smiles.

(You have to decide.)

n2.text:
(You lower your hand.)

(He bursts into tears and falls forward into your arms, his whole small body shaking. You hold him and let him cry.)

NOAH: Thank you. Thank you, thank you.

(His arms close around you, tight. Just for a moment, too tight.)

n3.text:
(You pick the iron bar up from the floor, the last piece of the old beam, black and heavy.)

Noah looks at it, then at you, and nods very slowly.

NOAH: I understand. It's what I would do.

(He bows his head to make it easy for you.)

varianten.bond:
Noah kneels in the middle of the cellar floor, small, wet, shaking. The dry woman beside him has crumbled to dust.

(His head lifts. His eyes, for the first time all night, are clear and blue and young. He looks at you the way he looked at you when the record was playing.)

NOAH: You told me you'd tell me. So tell me. Is he gone?

(His hand reaches for yours.)

NOAH: Please don't hurt me. Please, I'll be good, I'll make you tea every day, I promise, please.

And behind his eyes, a long way back, something smiles.

(You have to decide.)

k7.ending_let.text:
(You carry him up the spiral stairs and out into the pale hours before dawn, past the dark windows of Lünen. He does not let go of your coat once.)

— The Nook, a little later —

(Noah puts the kettle on. He hands you a cup and smiles at you over the rim, a small shy happy smile.)

NOAH: You were so kind to me. Nobody has ever been so kind.

The tea is sweet and thick. After the third sip your arm will not lift the cup anymore. Your legs are very far away.

(You slide off the chair. The floor is warm against your cheek. He kneels beside you and takes your hand, almost politely, and bends your thumb back until it snaps.)

You can hear it. You can't make a sound.

NOAH: I really am sorry.

(The knife comes out from under the blanket.)

{{click.}}

He takes his time. He is so careful. The hands first, then the feet, then the rest, because the lake is hungry and the pieces have to be small enough to carry.

— Three days later —

They find you over the next three days. Mostly in the water. Mostly neatly.

(On the double bench by the playground, a man in a washed-out hoodie lifts his face to the sun and sighs with perfect contentment.)

k7.ending_slaughter.text:
(You pick up the iron bar. Noah looks at it, then at you, and nods very slowly.)

NOAH: I understand. It's what I'd do.

(He bows his head to make it easy for you.)

The first blow misses the neck and lands on the shoulder, and the collarbone goes.

{{KRACK!}}

You feel it in your own teeth. He screams, a high thin bright scream, like a kid who was promised it wouldn't hurt.

The second blow opens the side of his neck. He doesn't fall. He kneels there with the muscle and the white of the bone showing and blood jetting across the floor in warm slapping pulses, and he talks, quickly, in his own sweet voice.

NOAH: Please. Please, don't. I don't want to go back in the dark. I'll be good. Please let me live.

The third blow doesn't finish it, because the thing inside him pushes back. The iron skids off bone.

{{CLANG!}}

The bar rings in your hands, and each time it does, the real Noah begs a little more quietly.

(His jaw hangs. His tongue is showing.)

By the fifth blow he can only say "pl". By the seventh he only looks at you. It takes eleven.

(When the head finally comes away it rolls once. His eyes are still open, and they look relieved.)

You sit there in the warm wet for a long time, holding something that used to be a child.

— At that same moment, in Lünen —

(Every candle in the town goes out at once. A lot of people you never met start to cry with relief.)

k7.ending_3.text:
(You don't move. You don't say a word.)

The seconds pass and something in the cellar starts to change. Noah's smile slides off his face. His eyes roll, not looking at you, not looking at anything.

(His mouth opens and a hundred voices come out of it, small ones, big ones, the sweet one and the cold one and the one from the dark, all screaming over each other.)

NOAH (sweet): Mine!

NOAH (cold): No, MINE!

NOAH (dark): Let me OUT!

(His fingernails go into his own cheeks and drag down. The skin comes away in wet strips. He bites through his tongue and spits it on the floor. He drives his thumbs into his own eyes and keeps pushing. There is a soft pop, and a second. He doesn't stop screaming.)

His body starts to fight itself on the floor, one arm against the other, a knee driven into his own ribs until they crack. You can only stand there and watch three people kill each other inside one small body, one after another, with a patience that makes you sick. The last one to die is the quiet one.

— When it is over —

(Noah sits up. Where his eyes were, there are only red holes. His mouth is open and nothing comes out. He will never say another word. A long thread of blood and drool swings from his chin, and his hands flutter in his lap like moths.)

NOAH: Ah.

NOAH: Ah, ah, ah.

(In the voice of a very small child.)

He is still alive in there. He will be for a very long time.

k7.warn10.text: He is still on his knees and hasn't blinked. 'You're thinking,' he says softly. 'I can hear you thinking.'

k7.warn20.text: 'It's okay,' he whispers. 'It's okay if you can't decide. I can't either.' And, almost to himself, with a very thin smile: 'Take all the time you want. We have so much time.'

items.name: Lizzy's tin
items.text: A rusty biscuit tin with LIZZY scratched into the lid. Inside: a handful of old keys and a photograph of a woman with folded hands in front of a house, four people beside her, none of them smiling.

items.name: Church bulletin
items.text: A folded church bulletin, brown with age. On the back, a list of names. One of them has been crossed out so hard that the pen went through the paper.

items.name: Iron key
items.text: A small, cold key on a cord. It fits the postern door of the castle, and the people who wear it, wear it like a cross.

items.name: Silver locket
items.text: A tiny locket on a broken chain, found in the Nook. There is nothing inside it. Not even a hair.

items.name: Tesseract
items.text: A cube inside a cube inside a cube, each a different colour of dark. It weighs nothing until you hold it. Then it weighs exactly as much as a drowned thing.

items.name: Yellow note
items.text: A tight square of yellowed paper, warm to the touch. It was written in the hand of someone who knew you would come.

items.name: Iron bar
items.text: The last piece of the cellar's old beam, black and heavy. It looks like it has been used before.
